Tartry. THE MUSIC OF LABOUR. The banging of the hammer, The whirling of the plane, The crashing of the busy saw, The creaking of the crane ; The ringing of the anvil, The grating of the drill, The clattering of the turning lathe, The whirling of the mill; The buzzing of the spindle, The rattling of the loom. The puffing of the engine, The fan's continual boom, The clipping of the tailor's shears, The driving of the awl— These sounds of busy industry, I love—l love them all. The clicking of the magic type, The earnest talk of men, , The toiling of the giant press, The scratching of the pen; The tapping of the yard-stick, The tinkling of the scale, The whistling of the needle, (When no bright cheek is pale) ; The humming of the cooking-stove. The surging of the broom, The pattering feet of childhood, The housewife's busy hum; The buzzing of the scholars, The teacher's kindly call— The sound of active industry, I love—l love them all. I love the ploughman's whistle, The reaper's cheerful song, The drover's oft-repeated shout, Spurring his stock along; The bustling of the market man, As he hies him to the town. The hello from the tree top, As the ripened fruit comes down, The insy sound of threshers As they clean the ripened grain, The husker's joke and catch of glee, ' liseath the moonlight on the plain; The kind voice of the drayman, The shepherd's gentle call— The sounds of pleasant industry, I love—l love them all.

He will adver- tise largely :—" For half-a-crown I will disclose a plan 'whereby halfpenny postaee stamps can'bemade to do the work of penny ones.' His 'plan is perfectly simple, and cannot fail. Use two of them. A RALE GENTLF.3fAN.—Very odd, inclose% are the signs and tokens of well-bred folk, according to some critics. Mr. Ruskin once said that the lime of demarcation was freed by "the onion" a vee•etable the existence of which respectable people ignore, ewe perchance when it is sug- gested in a salad; but a quainter criticism was that of a certain Irish barrister, who is said to have defined a gentleman as "a man who ate jam With his mutton." COMPLETE IN Two Vounans.—The late Sing of Pruseia -once sent to an aide-de-camp, Colonel Malachowki, who eves brave but poor, a small portfolio. bound like a book, in which were deposited five hundred crowns. Some time afterwards he met the officer, and said to him, " Ah, well! how did you like the new -work 'I sent you?" 4' Excessively, sire," replied the coloneL read it with such interest that I await the second volume with im- patience." The king smiled, and when the Officer's birth- day arrived he presented him with another portfolio, similar in every respect to the first, but engraved, "Com- plete in two volumes." -Peoesteres.—The pleasures which are usually craved are those just beyond or barely within reach, and the painful efforts to grasp them often counteractthe delight they are supposed to impart. Meanwhile a thousand unutilised sources of pleasure are unconsciouely trodden under foot in the hot pursuit. Men, for instance, post- pone all thought of happiness until they pet rich; then they say they will begin to enjoy life; but .all the time life itself is slipping away, cheated of its natural and reasonable pleasures, and either their dream of 'wealth is never realised, or, if it is, too often the newer of enjoyment is gone. GOOD MANNERS IN TITS Housv.—The presence ofegood manners is nowhere more needed or more effective than in the household, and perhaps nowhere more rare. Wherever familiarity exists there is a tendency to lose the cheek upon selfish conduct which the presence of strangers involuntarily produces. Many persons who are kind and courteous in company are rude and careless with these whom they love best. Emerson says good manners are made up of petty sacrifices; and certainly nothing can more thoroughly secure the harmony and peace of the family circle than the habit of makingemall sacrifices one for another. Children thus learn good manners in the best and most natural way, and habits thus acquired will never leave them. Courtesy and kindliness will never lose their power or their charm • and while all spurious imitations of them are to be despised, their real presence should be honoured and cherished by all. A FINE BIT ser Reeler Scrseue.—One of the finest bits of rocky scenery I remember to have seen any- where is within three days' easy ride on the Northern Pacific Railroad, and on the road to Cooke City mines. A long valley of some twenty-four miles leads easily up to the divide, from the east fork of the Yellowstone, nar- rowing as it rises. Some seven or eight miles from Cooke, on the left as you ascend, a vast wall of basalt rises almost sheer from the bed of the stream. It cannot be less than 3,500 feet in height, and I should fancy is over a mile along its base. When I first looked up at it its great, dark breast was braided all over with a hundred milky, wavy, flashing waterfalls. For a week we had almost continuous rain' and these warm showers, for it was July, had hastened the destruction of the snow beds on its crown, and down to the valley fell or trickled, literally, hundreds of streams, separating, spreading, uniting, and spreading again, as they crept or thundered downward. No words can convey any idea of the mingled beauty and grandeur of falling water and im- movable basalt, when smitten by the glory of the setting sun. One autumn evening, two years after, we camped at the same spot. We were smoking the last pipe of peace before turning in, when one of our party noticed a clear light falling on the summit above us. As we watched, the light crept slowly downward; at first we scarcely realised that it was the moon. We were down, remember, in a veritable chasm, one side of which—the side before us—was about three thousand feet higher than the other, and thus the moonbeans lit up its edge long before they touched the little prairie at its feet, where our camp lay. A great belt of clouds lay on the I rocky ridge at our back, and athwart these the moon.. , light passed, casting their moving shadows on the great. I gray mirror we were looking up at. What grotesque shapes they took, as they wound and unwound their long ; There we sat and watched them, until at last such moonligiit p.s you can only see when you are almost seven thousand fee;above the damper, denser air in , which ordinary life is t 6 be sustained fell full into the I gorge,—Scribner's Magazinee C emir GRATIS TO ALL.—Tne Llie'swing important fact can- not be too frequently iinprtned upon the minds of suffering hemaaltv, that Mr, Greed, 1L8.P., of Bradt rd. has for some time part. an aw hope gotie fur evvur. If th' fooaks at used t' liv owu Manchester wur t' rise eawt o ther graves an walk abeaut th' streets ov th' place as it is to-day, they'd find a grate change, fur th' progress made is remarkable an th' improvement is really won- derful. Wi then went throo th' greenheamses an fernerys an bak agen into th' Eggsibishun where wi yerd anuther recital on th' organ, an at after we'd rested a bit wi went fur t' see th' illuminashuns in th' greawnds. Neaw, aw've read abeaut sich things be- foore, bu aw cudn't hay beleeoved at it wur possy- bel t' mak ev'rything luk so pratty. Wot wi th' lecktrik leet, an th' little lamps shining bike so monny stars heere an theere an ev'rywheere, it wiir ' welly as leet as day, an when th' Fairy Fountain en th' band began t' play, n th' wimmen ther white dresses began t' flit up an deawn, aw geet it into mi yed once or twice at wi wur r fairyland, till Ann I Jane reminded mi aw wur still r th' flesh bi axin' wot toime th' train went. Well, when aw looked at mi watch aw fund at we'd ony abeaut six or seven minutes t' spare, so wi hurry'd off as fast as wi cud, an when wi geet t' th' stayshun th' train wur not quite due, bu we'd barely sat deawn befoor it drew up, an wi geet into a carriage wheer ther wur sum yung men an wimmen singmabeaut th" Home over there," an a jolly lot they wur. Ann Jane soon made hersel awhoam an wur chat- tin an singin wi em direckly, an ev'rything went merryly on till one o' th' singers axt wot wur th' name av a stayshun we'd just passed, an when aw yerd anuther say at it wur Timperley, an that tie next stoppin place wud be Bowdon aw thot aw shud bay fainted away fur aw saw at once at we'd getten into th' wrong train. Well, t' mak a lung story short, wi wur takken bak agen to th' Eggsibishun, an after waitin sum toime wi wur sent on bi th' last train, landin in Warrikin just as th' clock o'er Trinity Church wur strikin twelve. As wi wur coomin whoam tif second toime, a mon i' th' carridge, talkin abeaut th' Eggsibishun, sed at if Heaven wur a naicer place it wud bi woth I gooin to, an if aw conclude this papper bi reckom- endin ev'rybody t' mak an effort an try an get to booath places, speshally th' latter, aw doant think at aw shall aw've given bad advoice.

div.head: TIE REVISION COURTS. PENKETH.
div.p: TIE REVISION COURTS. PENKETH.

A court for the revisiiTin—Of-ihi;7;oters' list for the town- ships of Penketti, Great Sankey, Bold, and Cuerdley was opened at the Crown Hotel, Periketk, on Monday tnerning, by Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister. The Liberals were represented by Mr. H. Roberts, Liberal agent, Warrington; and Mr. P.M. Campbell, Liberal agent for Newton Division. On behalf of the Cmservatives there were present Mr. Well- head, solicitor, Warrington; Mr. Holbrook, Conservative agent; and Mr. Hampsoe, Conservative agent, Warrington. The lists for Bold and Cuerdley were cpickly disposed of without anything of public interest arising from them. AN UNPUBLISHED CLAIM—While the lists for the town- ship of Great Sankey were being dealt with, Mr. Roberts asked the assistant overseer (Mr. John Cook) if he received an occupier's claim on the 19th for Mr. John Broadhurst, Ivy House, Great Sankey —Mr. Cook: I did.—Mr. Roberts: It is not published.—Mr. Cook: It is already on the list of owners.—Mr. Roberts said that was no reason why the cairn should not be published. He objected to the assistant overseer &seeming the duties of the revising barrister. The claim ought to have been published at the prooer time.— The Revising Barrister: That is so, no doubt.—Mr. Wall- bead : I think the assistant overseer has attempted to save your time, sir. (Laughter.)—Mr. Cook said when he found the name on the list he thought he WAS safe in not publish- hog it.-1 he matter then dropped. CLAIM BY Ma. C. E. PARBER.—A claim as an occupier was made by Charles Edward Parker, which was opposed by the Conservatives. In answer to Mr. Wellhead, Mr. Parker said he was on the lodger's list last year.—Mr. Well- head asked how could Mr. Parker make this claim when he was on the lodgers' list last year.—lbe Barrister: He is now claiming for a dwelling house.—ln answer to further ques- tions by Mr. Wellhead, Mr. Parker aril the house he WAS claiming for was in the Chapel-road, Penketh. He had oc- cupied it about sixteen months. He took it in June last year, and had been under rent for it since then. It was in October when he went to reside in the house, but be had paid rest for it since the 19th June.—Mr. Wallhead con- tended that Mr. Parker had not made out his claim, as he himself said it was not till October that became to reside in the house.—The Revising Barrister said that as matters. stood the claim had not been made out. Mr. Parker had I net occupied the house during the whole of the qualifying period; and mere paying of rent Was not good enough.—Mr. Parker pointed out that be took possession of the house in • June, and likewise of the garden and the fruits thereof. He had also furnished the house before he went to resi.e there.—The Revising Barrister said he would allow the vote. . . .

• A LODGER'S CLAlM.—Robert Edward Garnett claimed a vote ass lodger with his father, Mr. Robert Garnett, of Hall Nook, Penketh. The claim was opposed by the Con- servatives. In answer to Mr. Wellhead, the claimant said he was in the employ of the firm of Messrs. Garnett and Sons, cabinet makers. He could scarcely tell how many others resided in his father's house besides himself. (Laughter.) —Mr. Roberts 'marked that the house was a very large one, and in answer to his question, the assistant overseer for Penketh stated that the house was rated at £76 101 —ln answer to further questions, claimant said that he had a contract with his lather for furnished bedroom and the use of furnished sitting rooms. He paid his father £3O a year, £l5 for the bedroom and £l5 for the use of the sitting rooms. He made this contract about two years ago, and he had paid quarterly. He had receipts for the payments, but he had not brought them with him.—Mr. Wallhead asked that these receipts should be produced.—The Revising Bar- rister said there was a strong presumption against the crea- tion of votes in another person's hose, ter which a vote already existed, and he thought they must have the receipts. —Mr. Roberts pointed to the high ratal of the house.—The Revising Barrister said there was DO question of ratal. If a man took a large house and had five or six sons at home they should not have aye or six votes as lodgers, because they were really not lodge's in law or in fact. Such a thing was never contemplated by the Act. He should require all the receipts. and then be shouli consider whether or not he should amend the second column of the claim, which was incorrectly stated.—Mr. Roberts said that after this expres- sion of opinien by the Revising Barrister it was not worth while the claimant going for the receipts.—The c'aim was consequently disallowed. WARRINGTON (COUNTY).

On Monday afternoon Mr. J. T. Poard held a court in the parade room at the Bridewell, Warrington, to revise the lists of voters for the townships of Rorton-with-Glazebroek, Poulton-with-Fearnhead, Warriogton, and Woolston-with- Martinscroft. The Conservatives and Liberals were repre• tented as at the court held at Penketh in the morning. TRAVELLING FOR HIS VOTE.—A gentlemen named Mr. Thomas Ally claimed an ownership vote in respect to pro- perty at Hiaton-with-Olazebrook, which was allowed.—Mr. Ally said that he did not wish to claim anything for loss of time, but as be bad travelled forty miles be thought his travelling cxpeneee should be allowed.—The Barrister said be could only allow expenses in eases where persons who were on the lists were objected to. HARD LINES —Mr. Thomas Birchen, 4, Froghall-lane, claimed a vote in respect of property bought by him—Mr. Wallhead objec'ed on the ground that the time the pro- perty had been in the possession of Mr. Birchen was four days short of the qualifying period.—The Revising Barrie- ter said that in that case he must disallow the claim.—Mr. Birchall : You cannot squeeze those four days in, can you?

The advantages of free lending libraries are, and have been for some time past, so widely acknowledged and appre- ciated that it would appear superfluous to have to say any- thing in their favour. , I consider that a great injustice is done to the public of Warrington in placing a restriction, by way of a subecrip- lion, on the books borrowed from the circulating depart- ment ; e g., a burgess pays his quota of the rate to support and carry on the Library, when, if he cannot afford to meet the extra call upon his purse, he is oebarred the privilege of borrowing a book for home reading. This seems most un- fair, because those who are in good circumstances, and can afford to pay the subscription, are just the class of persons who are able to subacrite their one or two guineas to Mudie's or Smith's; yes, and are also able to buy books for themselves. Thus the poor ratepayer is heavily handi- capped, and has no chance of keeping abreast of his more fortunate neighbours. Warrington was one of the first towns in the king mm to have a public library; the library there being established in 1848 under the Museums Act of 1845, and yet we find that it is far behind other town libraries of more recent growth in availing itself of the advantages offered by mak- ing its circulating, department free. The Warrington Library has, therefore, been instituted considerably over a quarter of a century, and during that long period has accumulated a very fine stock of books, greatly, I should say, in excess of any other library in any town of the same size; and yet the other towns, where libraries have been started., commenced by allowing the public the free privi- lege of taking books to their own homes for perusal. September 29th, 1857.

THE MEETING ON THE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—Although unable to attend the Town's Meeting on Tuesday night myself. I was very eager to know the result, and am greatly pleased to find it was so successful for the advocates of a Free Library. The character and tone of the speeches were admirable, and the almost unanimity of the voting cannot fail to impress the authorities with the deep earnestness of the people in this matter. The conduct of his Worship the Mayor too, was John Pickmere to the let- ter, and doubtless tended largely to produce the orderliness, geniality, and good humour which prevailed throughout the proceedings. One point made by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, which I sin afraid has been entirely overlooked by no, pleased me es- pecially, namely, the utter absence at present of any proyi- sian for the accom:nodatior. of the non-subscribing portion of our female population. Why should our wives and daughters be debarred the privileges which such an institu- tion is intended to confer t monstrousty unjust, met ought rw tenter tt.> be tulgrated. I gui wbeN, Were be OPPOnents to this Free Library scheme ? We have heard much of them from time to time, Ascl up to the present they have effectually prevented or de- layed the accomplishment of our object. But why do they not come forward and discuss publicly the question with us? In your last issue you gave theta a very cordial invitation to a so, and their refusal to comply betokens either a want of courage or inability to answer the arguments put forward in favour of the scheme. However, having failed to come forward at that meeting and show publicly some jast cause or impediment wily this scheme should not be carried into effect, it is only fair to say that they ought ever after to hold their peace. Bat now the question arittee—what next ? Well, to my mind there is nothing more needed than for the Town Council to ratify and carry into practical effect the resolu. tion which was proposed by Mr. Thomas Morris. Let it not be forgotten that this is the second time that a Town's Meeting called by the Mayor has given most emphatic ex• pression to the people's desire for a Free Li.brary in ite truest and most popular sense. The decision of the Council will be !trolled for with keen anxiety, and the action of emit in- dividual member clesely scrutinised. The way km been made clear and easy for them, e.nd there ought to be no difficulty in the matter providing there is to Will to do it, rim your figures unchallenged, your "47guments un- answered, and the Mayor almost persualvd. On their de- cision must our future action depend. Meanwhile we have but to watch and wait in the assuratte that "If it be now 'tis not to come, if it be not to come it will be now. If it be not now, yet it willt ome ; the readiness is all."— Yours, &c., A. RATHBONE, Arpley-st, Warrington, tre'pt. 29,1837. THE WARRINGTON LIBRARY.

"Giallo whispered, Sweet above God ever guarantees this Now: "—E. B. Browning. Not in the oak room, but in the library, sat Mrs. Desmond, Hyacinth kneeling at her feet, Vincent Lorraine standing by, his arms folded, his lips set. Mrs. Desmond was speaking, gently c,arressing her child's soft hair. "You ask a great thing of me, Mr. Lorraine, and I know you will forgive me if I speak plainly, for there is too much at stake for those reserves which otherwise courtesy would impose. Hyacinth is a mere girl, far younger in many things than the society-bred girls to whom you have been accustomed. She knows little or nothing of your world; she has not been taught to look lightly upon vices which men of fashion are accus- tomed, I understand, to call by any and every pretty name but those which rightly belong to them. With what credentials of the past do you come to ask me to give into your keeping my child's life? Your own life has been—admittedly--wild and reckless; what guar- antees for the future do you offer? It is easy to make promises when love is young, but will it be so easy in the more sober time to keep those promises? Does sin so readily resign its grasp on a man's heart and soul?" There was a moment's silence before Lorraine answered steadily— "Mrs. Desmond, you are just. For the past I can only ask forgiveness—unmerited, I own. For the future 'I have but three guarantees to offer--love— honour—gratitude. I will make no excuses—plead no palliation. I own that I set at naught your authority —that if Hyacinth had not come to me last night I should defy it still; but when she gave her life for me, trusted to me her fair name, all was changed. I had before demanded her hand, if not her love; but now I could not even ask forgiveness; she gave it freely because she loved me, and perhaps she trusts blindly." It must have been a base nature to which that speech was not an almost irresistible appeal, though not in- tended as such. The very disdain of all subterfuge. though the man's whole future was at stake, gave out the ring of the true metal. He might have pleaded eloquently, but he did not; he might have been prolific in promises, but he gave none. He sparned all but the mighty plea—love—gratitude—honour. Mrs. Desmond paused, looked down at the trembling form at her feet, then said slowly---- "Jf I should say that Hyacinth is too young to give to you--if I should ask you to wait—a few years—" She pawed again, and looked up into the handsome face ; it had gone white to the very lips. but there was not a word nor a movement—not the quiver of an eye- ; but suddenly Hyacinth sprang to her feet, and turned to her lover with outstretched hands in a kind of terror, and he had neither will nor power to resist that appeal. He locked the girl passionately to his breast, and bent his face to hers in silence; and for full two minutes that silence was unbroken. Then Mrs. Desmond, rising too, said gently and half archly— "When the garrison rebels, the city is given over to the enemy. Hush! no word now, Hyacinth! come to me presently—when Vincent Lorraine can spare you." And she went out ritnickly, leaving them alone. Vincent Lorraine had fought the battle with his tenants and won it; for the last experience of the landlord's indomitable will was enough for the most rebellions. Of the trio who had originated the con- spiracy that ended so disastrously, two were killed; Dermot Grady tried to escape, but he was found hiding behind the corn sheaves in his barn, and when the con- stables dragged him out, lo! a girl's hat lay among the rubbish, and Grady uttered a hoarse cry, while one of the constables held up the hat laughing. "Done for, me bhoy," he said; "that proves the young lady shpoke thrue ; she heard ye plottin' it all. The gaine's up wid ye! Before that night a dozen men were lodged in gaol, and the next day all over Ireland and England the newspapers were full of the siege of Curramore, and the extraordinary intrepidity of a young Irish lady. In the London clubs nothing else was talked about, and many who had told Lorraine he was playing a losing game in trying to reduce his tenants to order, owned that once more that strongly-willed Young man was right. He never failed when once he had made up his mind to gain a particular end; and of course the gossips did not fail to add that the beauty of the next season would be Irish, and her Christian name Hya- cinth. _ _

...... Mrs. Grady went up to Curramore, where Mrs. Des- mond and Hyacinth remained for the present, and tried all her eloquence to induce Lorraine to let her stop at the farm, but he was immovable. He knew, he said, that though she might not openly countenance murder she was aware her husband intended to commit it. He intended to clear the land of all the "bad blood," but he would give her ample funds to emigrate, and from that position nothing would stir him. A little later Dan Murphy reported all the tenants only anxious to " kape well wid Misther Lorraine." They loved him none the better, but they feared him thoroughly, and that was all Lorraine had contended for. Love he knew he could not win, even if be had sought it, and it scarcely squared with his haughty temper to conciliate; but fear he meant to inspire, and he had succeeded. The rioters were removed to Dublin for trial, the excitement in the district and the sympathy with the men prohibiting any chance of a fair trial at Roscom- mon. The evidence was damning, and Grady and his associates in the assassination plot were condemned to long terms of penal servitude. For the others Lorraine himself interceded, and they were allowed to escape with a year's imprisonment. Tracy Mansfield had disappeared. That young man wisely betook himself to a period of foreign travel under another name. It would be many, many years before he could show him- self at Ballygoyle again, for the people were justly indignant that a ringleader should escape while his followers met with punishment. And Dorine O'Conor had to reconcile herself as best she might to Hyacinth carrying off the prize. It was the bouquet that did it, she felt sure, she said, covering vexation with a joke; there was always luck in sevens. But Hyacinth thinks it was something more than "luck" that made her Vincent Lorraine's wife, and he thinks there was something more than luck in the stern resolve that took him to the wilds of Connaught. Hyacinth has been to Paris, and Vienna, and Rome, and climbed the Alps, and looked on the glories of Milan, and floated down the Grand Canal in a gondola. and everywhere men have bowed before her, and even beauties have been compelled to allow her just claim to homage. And is she changed in anything that made her essential charm? And has Bride Desmond, await- ing the wanderers in the stately English home among the beeches, cause to fear that the glamour is fading, and that Vincent Lorraine will turn back to the reck- less life cast behind him the day he gave Hyacinth Desmond his love? ~-• . - The sun is shining down on dreamlike Sorrento, and on two figures seated side by side on a little jutting -o;.2f4'.i:o.ck—a, man and a girl. She is bending over letter, anl-te-iS-Viiteiling her with a soft smile in his dark eyes that speaks his whole heart. Suddenly she drops her hands on her knee, and looking up quickly, meets his gaze, and colours under it as she would have done six months ago. "Well, sweetheart," he says, and the smile travels to his lips, "you have some good news in your letter. May I share it ?" "Of course." She put the letter in his hand. He read rapidly7.smiled again—then laughed. " TerenCe has been is laggard knight; but he has secursea pretty Aileen at last. And you want to go and dance at the wedding?" " Oh, Vincent!" with a rpilek-drawn hHath, "you always read my thoughts. I hardly liked to ask it— volt have never done anything but make my wishes -paramount. You will make me selfish—indeed you Will. lam not the saint you think me." "Are you not?" saidthe, Tlassing his arm round her and drawing her to him. `` Then a saint must be some- thing I cannot at all COMprehend and have no wish to encounter. And as 'for selfishness, perhaps lam sel- fish in 'making your wishes paramount, for your wishes are--must be--mine. I cannot help Iltrat, Hyacinth; lean no ,pore alter it then I can alter the harmonies of Music. "I know you cannot," the girl whispered, tremu- lously. a Bet, you make me too happy, Vincent. lam frightened sometimes.' "Too happy! Then indeed should I fear also, sweetheart, for you give me hack ten thousand-fold for all I give you. But I can face the knowledge that trouble-must surely come to both when I know that it can never touch your love or mine." He lifted her face to his own, adding softly: "You have changed the whole current of my life emd thoughts; you came to me like a dream of inless days. I could never be
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was hold at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Darbyshire, Greening, W. Houghton, Isher- wood, Clarke, Swinton, J. Houghton, Ratcliffe, hokersley, Mackie; S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE HOUSE COMMITTEE.
At a meeting of the above committee, held on the 16th September, it was recommended that Mr. Fletcher's tender for drapery be accepted.—The minutes were agreed to.

THE SCHOOLS COMMITTHB.—APPOINTMENT OF SCHOOLMISTRESS. At a meeting of the Schools Committee, held on the 27th September, Mr. Owen reported that Mr. Beckett, of Hart- ford, had completed his contract for flagging, dm. It Was recommended that the sum of £94 be paid on account. Miss Gawthorpe (Manchester), Miss Cox (London), Miss McEvey (Portsmouth), and Miss Welch (Norbury), ap- peared before the committee with reference to the appoint- ment of schoolmistress. The committee recommended the appointment of Miss McEvoy, who would appear before the Board at that meeting.—Mr. Mines produced his list of fur- niture, &c., required. The committee having inspected the ' various rooms, recommended that the liet as amended be adopted, and that Mr. Mines obtain tenders for the same.— The doctor reperted the general health of the children to be good.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the committee, remarked with respect to the fur- niture that the necessity for it bad arisen in this manner: There was no provision made in the first instance for the furnishing of the rooms, and the officers brought their own furniture. Thera had been some changes lately among the officers, and they had taken their furniture with them, and the officars who were coming had no furniture, and the committee had, therefore, been obliged to provide it for them. The committee had the four candidates before them, went carefully through the testimonials, and they decided to recommend the appointment of Miss McEvoy.— Mr. GREENING seconded the confirmation of the minutes, aed they were agreed to.—Miss McEvoy was subsequently called into the room, and informed of her appointment. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee fees were allowed in 17 new cases and 55 old.—Mr. ISHERWOOD asked if Inquiries , were made with regard to the fees allowed. They seemed to be growing every fortnight, and same people were gran- ted an extension of time. Was it possible to know how many people who were summoned before the magistrates at the Borough Police Court had fees paid by the Guardians ? He felt satisfied that some of the persons who were HUM. Monad had their fees paid by the Guardians. If they could afford to pay a fine for not sending their children to school they could afford to pay the school fees. (Hear. hear.)—Tne CHAIRMAN: I presume the committee have tbdt Information before them before they deal with the OREENING thought that all, inquiry that was possible to be made was made by the 9facer, It was guile true, as Mr. Isherwood had NO, that there were people, summoned before the magistrates for not vmding their chil. I • dren m school who had the school fees paid to them. As a member of the School Attendance Committee of the Corpo- ration, he had on various occasions recommended people to apply for school fees when the oommittee had been con- vinced that they could not possibly pay themselves ; but if the children did not go to school the fees were not paid. They were only paid on behalf of children attending school. No money was paid when the children did not go to school. The poor people did certainly get the five shil- lings to pay the fines which were inflicted upon thermbut how they got it was net a matter with which they bed to do. No doubt some one was punished most dreadfully in order that they might pay the fines.—The CHAIRMAN thought the explanation was quite satisfactory.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : You get a return in doubtful cases from the employers 7—Mr. GaumviNd We de.—The CHAIRMAN: This question has been broeght before the Board more than once, and the ex- planation which hoe been given by Mr, fawning has been given before. At the gatte time, Mr. Isherwood has only done his duty in bringing the matter before the Board. I thihk the question has been satisfactorily dealt with. (Hear, bear.)—Mr. GREENING: If any member of the Board has any information to impart the committee would be delighted to hear 11.—The minutes were then agreed to. Cave tar The Matron, in her joui nal, expreased thanks to the Bold. Street Weslevans for the fruit they bad sent for the sick in the hospital.

THE GUARDIANS AND THE INFIRMARY. Some discussion took place with regard to the case re- ferred te by Mr. Isherwood, of a man who had sustained in- juries in the Runcoin Union, but who bad been brought to the Warrington Infirmary, whence, after being attended to, be Was sent to the Workhouse.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON asked if they could not make a charge upon the Runcorn truer- diens for the expense incurred in this case.—The ASSISTANT CLESIC said they could not unless they got a proper order for his admission to the Workhouse, and the chances were that after the man got well again he would leave the neighbourhood. His OIVII private opinion was that these cases should be treated in the Infirmary.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said that was why he raised the queetion.—Tbe CHAIRMAN said he supposed sill Unions suffered more or less from cases of thi k d. The initial mistake was made by those who brought the man from one Union to another.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE was of opinion- that. the man ought to have stopped at the Infirmary when he was delivered there.—Mr. IsHER- WOOD said the man had been made a pauper by the fact of the Infirmary authorities sending him to the Workhouse in- stead of keeping him at the Infitmaiy, which was supported by public subscription.—lt wae in the end decided that the Cleik should write to the Infirmary authorities to see if it could not be arranged that cases of the kind ieferred to could not be treated there till they were tit to be sent back to their own Unions.

AN ECCENTRIC INMATE. It was stated by the Workhouse Master (Mr. Ward) that a man named Halligan had been received into the Work- house on an order of the Newton magistrates. The man was not certified to be a lunatic, but he really was one, as he wandered about Ma ridiculous fashion, and that morning he was found to have seven stockings on, while other in- mates were hunting about for their stockings. (Laughter.) THE WORKHOUSE NURSE. The ASSISTANT CLERK said there had been eighteen ap- plications for the post of nurse at the Workhouse.—lt was decided to refer these applications to the House Committee for consideration.

A SMALL MATTER. A letter waft read iron the Secretary's Office at the Royal Infirmary, Manchester, stating that Matthew Bracegirdla, a patient in the Indimary, from the Warrington Union, re- quired a supply of clean linen.—The AssterAwr CLERK said he had written back to say that two sets of clean linen were sent with the patient. In response to this ha had re- ceived the following letter from the Royal Infirmary :—" It is quite correct that two seta of clean linen were received with this patient, but as no arrawgementa have been made by your Union for the cost of washing the clothes they have of necessity been accumulating in the soiled state. The lad is at the present time wearing linen which belongs to this Infirmary, so that you will quite understand our writ- ing for a further supply. If your Guardians will say the clothes may be put out to wash at the expense of toe Union I will see that this is done, and thus obviate any incon- venience in the future." (Laughter.)—The ASSISTANT CLERK said he had written to say that the Union would be responsible for the washing of the linen. THE NEWTON VACCINATION STATION. The A:SISTANT CLERK said he had written to the Secre- tary (Mr. W. Haselden) of the Newton Polling District Conservative Club with regard to the heating of the club, which was used as a vaccination station. He said that un- less scmething was dons to obviate the complaints as to the ineufficient heating for the coming winter months they should be obliged to give notice. To this he had received a reply that the club managers could not undertake to make any alterations unless the Guardians agree to nay more rent. —Mr. CLARKE thought that the room ought to be inspected. —Mr. RATCLIFFE said be was given to understand that the room was sufficiently heated for any purpose, and it was in a very central place.—The CHAIRMAN suggested that the matter should be referred to the Newton Relief Committee, and this was agreed to. VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN. Mr. CLARKE asked if the clerk had received any commu- nication from the Local Government Boatd with regard to the vaccination returns.—The ASSISTANT CLERK : No:. Ea present —The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Clarke had sent in a notice of motion to the effect that the word " de.crinin,d be left out of placards posted at Earlestown lath regard to : vaccination. Mr. CLARKE said the Tentlon had refer- ence to the statement on the placards that the Guardians were "determined" to enforte the Vac- cination Act. That .wor':‘ did not represent bis feeling as one member of ttat Board, and he believed it did not represent the feeli:ags of other members besides. He thought that if the Gue,-dhlus procerly understood the Vaccination question at 2atkstown, if they were acquainted with all the I circumstances, they would not be so determined to enforce these Acts. Be therefore gave notice that he would move the resolution referred to at the next meeting of the Board. This,was all the business of public interest.

SINGULAR MANSLAUGHTER CASE AT BOOTLE.—On Tues- day, a coroner's jury, at Bootle, returned a verdict of man- slaughter against Daniel Madge, under singular circum- stances. The man quarrelled with his landlord, whose wife the day before had been confined. She got out of bed to separate the combatants, and was pushed out of the house on to the footpath, and from the shock and exposure died in the Bootle Hospital. THE ASSOCIATED CRAMBERs OE COMMERCE. The autumnal meeting of the Associated Chambers of Commerce was Opened on Tuesday at Exeter, under the presidency of Sir Bernhard Samuelson, M.P. The President, in his ad- dress, congratulated them on the revival of trade, as shown by the Board of Trade returns. The meeting proceeded to discuss the questions of railway communication, technical education, the currency question, ttc. During the day the tayor welcomed the Chambers to Exeter, and in the even- ing there was a reception by the local Chamber.

FOREIGN NEWS.

FRANCE AND GERMANY.—ANOTHER - FRONTIER INCIDENT. Penis, SIINDS-r---3i lieutenant of Dragoons in the garrison of Luneville was fired at from across the German frontier while out shooting at Raon- snr-Plaine yesterday. The lieutenant, attended by a had just taken up his position near the frontier, iand the sport was about to commence when three shots were fired from the German territory, killing the keeper And shattering the lieutenant's thigh. No one was to!be seen near the soot whence the shots proceeded. This doctors who ha-re examined the wounds declare that they were caused by military rifles, and that the ampu- tation of the lieutenant's leg will be necessary. The incident has caused considerable excitement in the com- munes along the frontier. Pants' SUNDAY Numr.—From inquiries made into the affair at Raonsnr-Plaine, it appears that the shots which killed the gamekeeper and wounded the French offic,er of Dragoons while they were standing six or seven yards from the German frontier line, were fired by some German gamekeepers. The latter state that they , thought they had to do with poachers, who had paid no .1 heed to their repeated summonses to surrender. Pains, Mownar.—The new frontier incident has taken such an important aspect that Count Munster called to- day on M. Flourens, and spent with him three-quarters of an hour going into the report of the Procurator-gener- al of Nancy, who sent to Raon-sur-Plaine to inquire into this grave affair It is to be observed that while Count Munster has so far remained without any instruction the 'German authorities have ordered a searching inquiry ps.l into the shooting at Raon-sur-Plaine of Lieutenant Mangen and his game beater, Brignon, by Richard Kaufmann, a German forest guard. The latter is charged with firing from the German territory at a Frenchman on a path many yards on the French side of a row of frontier posts. It may be that Kaufmann is a stupid fellow, and did nob well take in the territorial boundary and what it -meant, but it is a dangerous state of things when ' the forefinger of a German forest guard is, as he ' looks into France, so nenr the trigger of his rifle. Wangen's companions at once ran up, calling, as they 'did so, to the Germans in ambush, who they thought must have been sportsmen like themselves, to cease firing. They then saw one German uniform and then another. :Their exasperation was such that they -wonder they did not go and shoot both. After binding up as well as they could the wounds of Brignen, who was writhing in agony, and died after five hours of intense suffering, they went to fetch from a gentleman's house close by a lightly-hung vehicle in which the wounded men were taken for surgical aid to Raon-les-,Seau-x. Brignon there died, and it was found that the ball that hit him was that of a German soldier's rifle. UNSETTLED STTUATION qN BULGARIA.—

Tap POWERS AT VARIANCE. PrrEasntrno, MONDAY.—Yesterday's Moscow Gazette says that if Prince Bismarck and Count Kalnoky, at their Meeting at Friedrichsruhe, dreamed of resuscitating the absurd plan of dividing the influence in the Balkan Peninsula between Austria and Russia they will be disap- pointed. Russia will never give up her position gained by a policy pursued tor centuries and involving great sacrifices. Russia, adds the Gazette, ought to maintain her present attitude unfettered by any engagement. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY.—A steamer, which is believed to contain persons disaffected to the Bulgarian Government, has been seen during the past two nights hovering off the Routnelian coast': near Bourgas. Strict watch is kept on shore, and if a landing be effected the invaders will probably find the whole population pre- pared to resist them. , SOFIA, MormAY.—The whole of the Powers have agreed to accept the proposal of Turkey. thus modified, that' instead of a Russian Licutenalit Prince being sent to Bulgaria an international commission shall be formed under the presidency of an Ottotnan delegate. It is thought, however, that this scheme will be resisted by the Bulgarians.

div.head: NATIVE REVOLT IN THE CAROLINE
div.p: NATIVE REVOLT IN THE CAROLINE

MADRID, MONDAY EVENING:—IIIIE'IIigeDee to hand from Manilla gives a serious account Of the state of affairs in the island of Ponape, one of the Caroline group. The natives rose in revolt in protest against the expulsion of an American missionary. , They killed the Spanish governor, and also, it is stated, massacred the entire garrison, with the exception of two, who escaped, and took refuge on an English schooner. A Spanish man-of- war has been sent to the island, and will exact stern vengeance.

NEW ZEALAND ELECTIONS.—THE PRE- MIER DEFEATED. WELLINGTON (New ZEALAND), TUISDA4.—The general elections to the House of Representatives took place throughout the colony yostierday. The general result is not yet known, The Hon. Sir Robert Stout (Premier) and the Hon. J. A. Tole (Minister of Justice) have, how- ever, been defeated. The other Ministers have been re-elected, as have also Mr. H. A. Atkinson, Mr. Hall, and Sir G. Grey. '

OUTBREAK NEAR RANGOON. The Times corresp;ndent at Rangoon telegraphs: A somewhat serious outbreak has occurred at Kyouktan Police Station, within a few miles of Rangoon. Fifteen prisoners charged with dacotty rose, and overpowered the police guard, killing two of them, and, wounding several others, and then made their escape, carrying off the police rifles and d large quantity of ammunition. Reports from Mandalay arc unsatisfactory. A fresh rebellious conspiracy has been detected and crushed.

div.head: TERRIBLE SCENE.
div.p: A TERRIBLE SCENE.

A fearful scene was witnessed on Lake Superior and is reported in edvices just received at LiverpooL During the recent gales which caused such terrible havoc to shipping on the American aeaboard, the large schooner Niagara with 1,400 tons of ore on board, left Ashland in tow of the steam barque Australasia. When off Whiteash Point the tow rope parted. The Niagara was then struck by a heavy sea and thrown on her beam ends. Those on board the barque were powerless to help the vessel or the poor people on board. The next instant the Niagara was in the trough of the sea, and then with awful rapidity she eppeared on the crest of a tug t wave. A tremendous Crash followed, and. those on board the barque beheld the spars and masts of the Niagara being hurled on to the deck. Captain Clement and his crew were next seen endeavouring to cut away the wreckage. This was futile, and for safety the men went into the cabin. A yawl boat on deck was then launched, and into it all of those on board the Niagara scrambled. The crew numbered 15 hands, and besides these there were several friend eof Captain Clement who were seeing him off. The exact number was not known. The small craft had only got a few yards off when a sea struck and capsized it. The waves were fearful and the unfortunate people could snake no _

Bfillt against them. The men were seen struggling for their lives and crying for help which could not be afforded them. In a few minutes all was still save the roaring of the wind and the waves. Not one of those on board the Niagara was saved. THE AMERICA CUP RACE. NBR YORK, TUESDAY EVENING.—The Thistle crossed the line a minute ahead of the Volunteer at 12 34 p.m., but thirteen minutes later the Volunteer was leading on the starboard tack, and ten minutes afterwards was a quarter of a mile ahead of the 'I histle. Although the wind was only Lowing at the rate of three miles an hour the Volunteer continued to gain rapidly, and at 3 45 she rounded the Sandy Honok lightship—the turning point— three miles ahead of her rival, which was 16 minutes behind at that point. In returning the Thistle failed to improve her position, and the Volunteer won the first of the races easily. NEw YORK, 11 6 Pat.—The Volunteer passed the win- wing line at sh. 25m. 305., and the Thistle at sh. 44m. 455.; the American yacht thus winning by 19m. I'ss. The course covered in yesterday's race for the America Cup is as follows :—Starting from just below Bay Ridge, the yachts proceeded through the Narrows to the south-west Spit and Arno buoys, fixed there, to buoy 5, off Sandy Hook, which they passed on the outside. The outer mark is off Sandy Hook lightship, and from this point the yachts returned by the same course,finishing at buoy 15. off Port Wadsworth. INTERNATIONAL SCULLING MATCH.

NEW YORK. THVESDAY.—A three mile sculling match between Courtney, the American nutter, and Enbear, of Binghamton, New York State, has resulted in the defeat of the Englishman. TERRIBLE GITNP')WDER FXPLOSION. TWELVE MEN KILLEU.

A Central News telegram, dated Vienna, Thursday, flayS:—A terrible explosion took phice yesterday evening at the Goveroment Gunpowder Factory at Felixdorf, near Vienna. Twelve men were killed and the building was Wrecked.

SHOCKING MURDER IN KILICENSIi.—A farmer named Meagher, who resided at Brookawan, county Kilkenny. has been found iu a ditch, with his body mutilated, haying evi- dently been murdered. There were indications close by of a severe struggle haying taken place. Sin W. HARCOURT AT LEWES.—Sir William Harcourt addressed a crowded meeting of Liberals at Lewes on Wed- oesday night and met with a hearty reception. Ile ridiculed Lord Randolph Churchill's notion that this had been a Jubilee session in regard to legislation. Lord Raa- ,„il°lPh might bold that view. hut then be agreed with no. body, and Sir William preferred to call it a carnival of 'coercion. However, if this policy of violence was continued Liberals would soon return to power under Mr. Gladstone, justice would then be done to Ireland, and other legis- lation would progress. The Government had a dwindling znlajority, and the country were looking for their nuccessors 11.4 office. A little more violence, imprisonment, and shoot- ing would get rid of the Ministry. They were told Ireland wanted 20 years of firm government ; that simply meant 20 Years of M tchelstownism, which humane Englishmen paid not tolerate. Rack-renting had done mach mischief. had smoked bees out of the hive and stolen the honey. ,4eas to the Unionist party, there was no room for thett un- -1 s they returned to the fold. They were now simply a 'ort of tin kettle tied to the tail of the Tory Government. Itne battle now was that of freedom, conciliation, and sit- against privilege and force.
EXTRAORDINARY MUTINY AT LIVER-
POOL-A REFORMATORY SHIP HELD BY LADS

A serious mutiny occurred on Sunday, on the reforma- tory: ship Akbar, anchored in the Mersey. The officers, it as stated, were for a time overpowered. and the mutineers were for five hours in full possession of the vessel. Seventeen of the lads lowered a boat and made their escape, but nine of the number have been re-Cap- tured by the Liverpool police. Most of them were de- tained on the Akbar under convictions from Liverpool. Captain Symons was on leave last week, and during his absence some of the bigger lads broke into his cabin, and stole a. quantity of jewelry and other valuables. The ringleader also endeavoured to induce other lads to revolt, and on Saturday there were many signs of in- subordination, when it became known that the boys who had broken into the captain's cabin would be severely punished for their offence. On Sunday there were several Minor breaches of dis- cipline. early in the day, and in the afternoon insub- ordination was openly manifested. The chief officer and schoolmaster endeavoured to conciliate the lads, and were successful for a time, but after tea the disturbances were renewed. The chaplain then endeavoured to in- fluence the lads, but without result, and there was a scene of great uproar, the lads shouting defiantly and running all over the ship. The police were sent ashore, but the lads became worse, and 17 of them lowered a boat and rowed to the shore. Officers went in pursuit.hut the lads ,escaped. There were 150 lads on board, and only six officers, the others being ashore on leave. The lights were put out and great damage was done to the vessel before the mutiny was quelled. On Monday, the prisoners, whose ages ranged from 16 to 19, were charged before the Stipendiary, some with theft of jewelry and absconding from the ship, others with simply absconding. Moffatt and Wilcox, the ring- leaders, were said to have been persecuted on board the vessel, and the officers were always at them. The pri- soners were nearly all Liverpool boys, one of them being a petty officer' another a library boy. The prisoners were remanded. Three more of the mutineers of the reformatory ship Akbar have been arrested, and were on Tuesday remanded by the Liverpool magistrates. One of the prisoners gave another boy a bracelet, which has been identified as a portion of the property stolen from the captain's cabin, which was looted.

• DESTRUCTIVE FIRES. A fire broke out on Monday morning, about half-past one o'clock, in an extensive paper and printing factory, be- longing to Messrs. Ashdown and Hobday, at Dover, The whole of the factory was destroyed, together with some 'very valuable machinery, and about £2,000 Worth of Government paper. A private house adjoining was also burnt, the inmates having narrow escapes. A constable was injured by a falling wall. The damage amounts to £20,000.

Shortly after work was commenced on Monday, at the Bow-street Spinning Mill. Bolton, a fire broke out in the third room from the head-stock of a mule, and spread with alarming rapidity from floor to floor, causing great consternation amongst the workpeople, who fled helter- skelter from the building. With the prompt arrival of the borough fire brigade the flames were checked, and in an hour were extinguished, but not before damage had been done to the extent of £2,000, which is tully covered by insurance in several offices. Jacobs' clothing establishment at Cinderford, the largest clothing establishment in the town, was partially destroyed by tre on Sunday morning. The damage done amounts to considerably over £l,ooo.—At half-past one no Sunday morning a large paper mill at Buckland, Dover, occupied by Messrs. Ashdown and Hobday, was totally destroyed by fire. A police constable was injured by falling debris—On Saturday night a fire which caused great damage broke out on the premises of Mr. Kiernan Egan, town councillor of Birr, Ireland.—Damage amounting to about £ll,OOO was caused by the fire which, on Saturday night, destroyed the premises of Sylvester and Son, firrniture warehousemen, Chelsea.—A fire broke out at midnight on Saturday, in the brew- house of the Prince of Wales Inn, Ledbury. Of the three men who were sleeping in the room above one escaped through the window, but was seriously burnt. A young man named Ed ward Lancett, in trying to escape downstairs, fell into the fire underneath and was burned to death, and Richard Cale, a married man of the neighbouring village, was found dead by the Side of the bed.
THE HEXTIIORPE DISASTER AND THE • RAILWAY EMPLOYES. .

Over 300 officials employed by the Manchester, Sher- field, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, at Mexborough, which is an important locomotive centre, met on Sunday afternoon, to decide what the men could do for the com- pany under the circumstances of the Hexthorpe acci- dent. The meeting, by a large majority, aeCided to give the compsny a week's wages, it being stated that this :would cement the bond of unity which already subsisted between the employers and employed. A committee to consult with the other centres on the system was apnoiuted. The condition cf the patients in the Doncaiter In- firmary continues about the same. A runlour was cur- rent, on Monday, that Mr. Trimnell, of Ludgate Hill, '..ondon, was dead; but on inquiry at the infirmary the statement was contradicted, and it was announced that Mr. Trimnell is quite as well as can be expected. The most critical cases are Mr. Addy Thompson and Mrs. Stokes. The other patients are making satisfactory progress. It is stated on.tlio authority, of tliE consulting engineer of the Amalgamated Societylof Railway Servants that the officials of the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire Railway Company have refused to allow a number of experts to make an examination en the spot on behalf of the engine-driver and fireman, who stand committed for trial in respect of the terrible collision at Hexthorpe. On Tuesday, the county coroner. Mr. F. E. Nicholson, re- sumed his inquiry respecting the railway accident at Hexthorpe. The jury and officers first visited the scene of the disaster, the signals and train being shown as on the occasion of the accident. Major Marindin, Inspector of the Board of Trade, was again present. The Coroner aunounced that the head guard of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire train, W. EL Smith, for whoni the inquiry was adjourned, was still unable to attend. but after an inspection of the line they would have no difficulty in arriving at a verdict. Several witnesses, whose evidence was taken at the borough inquiry, were called. Mr. Warren, for the driver and fireman, complained that the company's solicitor would not supply him with a copy of the printed instructions, and further that Mr. Pol- litt would not allow him and a skilled witness- to inspect the wine and carriages of the Manchester. Sheffield, and Lincolnshire train.

Mr. harper denied that any impediment was thrown in the way of Mr. Warren's examination, and an angry altercation ensued between him and Mr. Warren, the lat- ter demanding that he should read the correspondence, when the Coroner interposed. Isaacs, the inspector of signals, stated that the flag signalmen were supplied with fog signals, but he could not say why they were not used. The pip, after deliberating 55 minutes, found that the collision was the result of ,culpable carelessness on the part of the driver and fireman of the Manchester, Shef- field, and Lincolnshire train, and that both were guilty of manslaughter.

that Mr. Harrington had withdrawn from the case, Mr. O'Brien addressed the magistra,es in justification of hie counsel's action, and then proceeded to reply himself to the evidence which had been given against him He charged the prosecution with resorting to foul play to establish their I case, and asserted that be gave the advice ke did deliberate- ly, and that instead of having committed a crime he had prevented crime. He concluded by saying that possibly ' before his prison hours were folly numbered—at all events, not very long after—the great appeal court of the English nation, who would be the ultimate judges of the matter, I would reverse the decision that would be pronounced that day, and declare it to be a crime no longer to defeod the , homes and assert the liberties of the Irish people. After Mr. Carson had replied for the prosecution Mr. Eaton de-I livered judgment, which was to the effect that Mr O'Brien should go to prison for three months on the charge relating I to the 9th August. The Court considered that this sentence I would be sufficient to cover the second cffence also, that of the 11th August; but Mr. Carson called evidence in this case too, after which the court passed another sentence of I three months'Amprisonment, the two sentences to run con- currently. Mr. O'Brien gave notice of appeal, and waslib- erated on bail. In the case of Mr. Mandeville. who was charged with a like offence, a sentence of two months im- prisonment was passed; but he likewise was liberated on ' bail, pending an appeal. Mr. O'Brien was loudly cheered after he left the court, hut there was no disturbance, the people dispersing quietly at the demand of Captain Plun- kett, which Was supported by the parish priest and several , of the Nationalist leaders. Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., addressed a meeting on Sun- day afternoon of the Mitchelstown branch of the National League. This is one ot the suppressed societies, and a good , deal of contrivance had to be resorted to to bold the meet- ing, which took place on private premises. Mr. O'Brien ridi- culed the efforts of the Government to put down the League. I He said he should have preferred to go through his impris- onment at once, but he knew that the next few , weeks I would be very critical weeks in Ireland, and he thotkht it his duty to be with the people as much as possible. He ad- vised them to continue to hold their meetings, and to fill the gaols if necessary.
