div.head: DESPERATE ENCOUNTER.
div.p: DESPERATE ENCOUNTER.

A serious encounter took place at Kilbarry, near 'Dun- naanway, on Monday, between a family named Hurley, whose cattle were being seited, and the sheriff's officer and police. When driving off the cattle the officers were attacked by the Hurleys and a crowd which had assembled with stwaes,s ticks, and pitchforks. A sheriff's officer named Cambridge, was injured, receiving a blow from a stone and two wounds from a pitchfork; and a constable also was stabbed with a fork. The police charged with fixed bayonets, and loaded their rifles, threatening to fire. This, however, had no effect in dispersing the crowd, who only became more incensed, and renewed their attack with increased vigour. Eventually, after a struggle, in which many blows were exchanged, the bailiffs and olice had to retreat, leaving the cattle behind. Two of the Hurleys (brother and sister) are wounded—one from a blow of a stick, and the other from a bayonet thrust. Prosecutions will be brought under the Crimes Act.

div.head: DISTURBANCE AT FERMOY.
div.p: DISTURBANCE AT FERMOY.

A disturbance took place on Saturday night at Fer- moy, in which a number of people were injured. Dr. Tanner, MP., was addressing a number of people, when a body of police came up and proceeded to clear the .square. Dr. Tanner at first questioned the right of the police to interfere, but eventually asked the people to move away. A conflict between the police and the people ensued, and the military appeared on the scene, when order was restored. ,Signs of another disturbance were visible all day, but stone-throwing did not commence on Sunday until seven in the evening, when a body of constabulary from Mitchelstown entered the place. On of the men received a very violent blow, and was knocked down and disabled. The Royal Hotel, the landlord of which is boycotted, and at which establishment Captain Plunkett and Mr. War- burton, resident magistrates, were staying, was subse- quently attacked, and many windows were smashed. The police, on interfering were stoned, but by the free ,use of their batons they succeeded in clearing the streets: More than 100 persons, rioters and lookers on. were in- 'lured in the struggle. Michael Hickey, over 60 years of age, who received a blow from a truncheon across his temple, lies at Barrack Hill in is precarious state. Twe young men, named Philip Ryan and John Buckley, were severely beaten, and received scalp wounds. A large number of bandaged heads were to be seen on Monday. The ill-feeling between the police and the people, con- sequent upon the exciting and disorderly scenes of Satur- day and Sunday, is growing in intensity, and further outbreaks are by no means improbable. Sunday's riot was a very fierce one, and so threatening was the situation at the period when the street fight- ing was at its height that the military were sent for. Beyond patrolling the streets, however, their ser- vices were not required, the reinforcements of constabu- lary which had arrived from Mitchelstown and the sur- rounding districts being found sufficient. MEETING OF SUPPRESSED LEAGUE BRANCHES. Meetings took place on Sunday of the suppressed branches of the National League at Woodford, Killeena- deema, Doniry' and Ballinakill. That at Woodford was the largest held for some time. Distriet-inSpeetae Murphy and a force of police were present, but the former simply cautioned the people, and asserted his right to be there. The police took notes of the procal• ings, and the names of a large number present including, Fathers Coen and Roche. At Doniry the police cautioned the people who, notwithstanding, held their, meeting, and the police were present. Neither at Ballinakill nor Killeenadeema were police at the meeting, but District- Inspector Davis went to the house where the meeting was held, and stated that he would prosecute the owner if it were allowed. At Loughrea, a body of constabulary guarded the entraqce to the League room, and cautioned those who entered. The proclamation was read over to the owner bf the room, and no meeting was held, the people acting oh ,the advice of the Rev. R. Meagher. It is understood in he district that prosecutions will be in- stituted against the priests and others who attended the Woodford meeting. Sunday being the usual day of meeting of Kilrush branch of the National League there a great number of people assembled in good time at. the building where the gatherings have always been held. A body of police marched up and down outside, and when the priests and the Town Commissioners arrived, amid great cheering, and the doof was opened, Head Constable Kennedy ad- vanced towards Fr. Mc.Kenna, and said" I warn all parties that if they go in to hold a meeting of the League they will be prosecuted." (Groans.) Father Mc.Kenna replied, "It is not a meeting of the League we are to hold, as that is suppressed, but, a meeting to explain to the people. Mr. Healy's letter to the leaseholders who want to go into the Land Court." The head con- stable thereupon asserted his right to be present, but Father Mc.Kenna objected to his doing so, as being both insulting and illegal. The people' with the priests, then entered the building, which speedily became crowded, and they were followed by the head constable and Sergeants Fletcher and Dee, who were re- , ceived with much groaning. Replying to Father Mc.Kenna, the police stated they were there by order of the Government, and, despite renewed objections, they persisted in staying, whereupon Father Mc.Kenna de- clared the meeting adjourned, and advised the people to disperse. The police were the last to leave. At Ballylongford, in county Kerry, on the other side of the Shannon, when the police tried to force their 'way into a meeting of the inhabitants, they were repulsed with sticks, amid great excitement. On Saturday 15 members of the committee of the

Woodford branch of the National League, together with Father Coen, Father Roche, and Father Egan, proceeded in a body to the rooms of the National League, where they were met by Head Constable Reynolds and six poliCemen, who at first prevented them- from entering . . . .
She was arrested, and, with Lane, aurally, and ins vrne' committed to Limerick prison, bail being refused. Crowds afterwards flocked to the scene, and great ex- citement prevails.
THE MITCHELSTOWN AFFRAY.

The inquest at Mitchelstowa on the bodies of the three men shot by the police—Shinnick, Lonergan, and‘Casey —during the affray on the 9th inst., was resumed yes- terday morning by Mr. Rica, coroner. Smt. Brennan, the first witness, who was in charge of 1-I,e police who went to the a.ssistance of the party pro- tecting the Government note-taker, said he was struck with a stone which cut through his helmet. He saw sr.veral policemen struck with stones, one being knocked down. Witness was struck with sticks several times about the body. • •

Cross-examined: Witness admitted striking a man with his rifle who tried to assault him, after the police re- treated to barracks. •District-inspector Irwin told the police to load and fire at the pople throwing stones. Witness fired one shot. He could not say if it took effect. The police apprehended that the barracks would be levelled over their heads. Witness contradicted the evidence given by Head Constable Doherty, who was protecting the reporter, and who stated that his party were not attacked. Witness further stated that he gave three ball cartridges to Sergt. Kirwan after the firing. Kirwan spoke falsely in saying that he got the cartridges before the firing ceased. Witness fired in the direction where the body was found in the square. He aimed to kill. This latter statement provoked groans in court, and the coroner was asked, but refused, to clear the court. The Coroner and Mr. Harrington stated that they had .recrived several threatening letters since the inquest animenced. but -would take no action.

div.head: GENERA]. NEWS.
div.p: GENERA]. NEWS.
Extensive farm buildings and the produce of 400 acres were destroyed by fire. near Fleet, on Sunday. The damage is estimated at £lO,OOO. •

The Mayors of the districts of Paris have received orders to send in lists of the German residents in their districts to the Ministry of the Interior. Mr. Gladstone read both lessons at Hawarden•Church on Sunday in excellent voice. The Rev. Stephen Glad- stone took the sormons for the first time since his return from his holidays. There was a large party of Americans among the congregation.

THE EXETER, THEATRE FIRE: ANOTHER DEATH.— Another of the victims of the recent fire at the Exeter Theatre, Mrs. Coombe, diel in the hospital on Sunday. She was the who of the check-taker in the gallery stairs, and had gone up to see her husband. The rush took place whilst she was there, and she was terribly injured in the panic. A distressing suicide is reported from Mountain Ash. Mr. Isaac Thomas, managing chemist, after opening his shop went back to bed, took a dose of prussic acid, and died immediately. The previous evening he went to a barber and asked for a clean shave, saying it was the last he should have. Ile leaves a young widow and children. No cause is assigned for the rash act.

CHARGE AGAINST A Posrsusran.—Robert J. Jones, postmaster of the Valley office, Carnarvon, has been charged at Holyhead with forging withdrawal notices. Only one case was gone into, involving a deposit of £lofl by a person who could not write, but it was stated that about 20 other cases have to be brought forfard. After formal evidence had been tendered, the magistrates granted a remand, accepting bail of £4OO.

At Nottingham, on Saturday, a shocking scene was Witnessed. While the workmen employed at the New- castle pit, Basford, were assembled, waiting to descend, William .Shares, aged 48, whose mind is supposed to have been affected, suddenly sprang from among the group, and jumped down the shaft, 130 yards deep. The body fell upon the bonnet of the cage at bottom, and was fearfully smashed: Sharpe leaves a widow and eight children. The Manchester County Stipendiary on Monday com- mitted Wm. Beasley for trial on two charges of attempted murder. On the 6th August the prisoner visited his sister, Mrs. Ludlam, and attacked her witii a shovel with- out any provocation having been given. She was ren- dered unconscious. A gentleman named Brooks, who was passing, interefered, and the prisoner struck him several times with a cleaver, inflicting such dangerous wounds that his life was despaired of. Professor Gould has ascertained that aiirial telegraph wires on poles .transmit electricity at the rate of from 14,000 to 16,000 miles per second, and that the velocity of transmission increases with the distance between the wires and the eneth—tiet•t is, with the height at which they are suspended. Subteitanean wires, like sub- marine cables, transtnit slowly: Wires suspended at a low elevation above the ground transmit signals at a speed of 12,000 miles per second. ' The present is the most prolific season ever known in Wales for mushrooms. Thousands of baskets have been sent to the markets daily. The quantity has so far ex- ceeded the supply of hampers that baskets, tubs, bucket, and all sorts of receptacles have been brought into use. The farmers have thus largely supplemented their regu- lar income. The price given by the dealers for,the early crop was 6d.; then, as the supplies increased, it dropped t 2 4d., then to 31, and now they are giving only 2d, per lb. SHIPPINO DigASTIM AND :SHRIOUS Los S LiVe.—Cla Saturday morning, Mr. Crawford, hon, secretary of the National Lifeboat Institutien at Margate, received a telegram stating that a PITO) fishing vessel was ashore on the Long Sand. Some men belonging to the lifeboat Quiver at once went out in the paddle steamer India, and when near the Kent ish Kneel: saw a raft on which were three men. They were rescued and landed at Mar- gate, where they made a statement to the effect that they were part of the crew of the dandy, Patrie, No. 1,031, of Feearnp. They left on board the captain and 16 men, all of whom it is feared are lost, as they had not left the vessebwhen she was seen to founder.

SRITING A HUSBAND ON FIRE ix BED.-011 Saturday, at West Bromwich, Sarah Parkes, Greets Green, against whom a coroner's jury haw; returned a verdict of wilful murder for causing the death of her husband by setting fire to the bed in which he lay drunk, was charged be- fore the magistrates with the crime. A woman who had lodged with the deceased and the accused deposed to hearing quarrels between them, and' the threat of the prisoner to burn the deceased on Hoe morning of the fire. After the fire she smelt paraffin oil in the bedroom, and saw dark spots on the Boor. About hal a pint of oil was also missing from a bottle which witness hal handed prisoner shortly before the occurrence. The house surgeon at the hospital to which Parkes was removed Stated that prior to his death be said he knew nothing of how the fire occurred. Ile woke up to find himself in flames. The man was badly burnt about the chest, arms, and thighs. Further witnesses were examined; and it was shewn in cross-examination that the deceased threatened the prisoner the same morning. She oleaded not guilty, and reserved her defence. The bench com- mitted her for trial for wilful murder. The case has caused considerable sensation in the district, and the oourt and its precincts were crowded. The number of steamers existing in the world last year was estimated at 9,969, of an aggregate burthen of 10,531,843 tons. The corrkoonding number of steamers existing in the world in 1865 was estimated at 9,642, of an aggregate burthen of 10,291,241 tons. The total of 9,969 steamers, representing the world's steam shipping In 1886 was made up as follows :—lron steamers, 8,198, of an aggregate bun l :len of 8,911,406 tons; steel steamers, 770, of an aggregate burthen of 1,206.962 tens; compo- site steamers, 109, of an aggregate burthen of 32,820 tons; and wooden steamers, 822, of an aggregate burthen of 380.655 tons. Of the steamers afloat in 1885, 5,792 were owned by the United Kingdom and its colonies, their aggregate burthen being 6,595,871 tons. The other countries of the world owned steamers as follows, last year:—Germany, 579; France, 509; ,Spain, 401; the , United States, 400; Norway, 287: Russia, 212; Denmark, 200; Italy, 173; Holland, 152; Brazil, 141; Japan, 105; Greece and Turkey 82 each; Belgium, 68 ; Chili and the Argentine Republic, 43 each; China and Porting-al, 27 each; Hawaii, 21; Mexico, 15; and miscellaneous, 50. It will be seen that, notwithstanding the great depression prevailing in steam shipping. the number of steamers afloat last year increased to the extent of 327, as corn- ",red with 1885.-lagiare,ie,t.

Two Mimi DROWNED.—WbiIat a barge named the Spar- row, belonging to the Union Lighterage Company, was going down the Thames on the ebb tide on Wednesday morning, it came into collision with Lambeth Pier. Two men who had been seen on heard the barge were shortly afterwards observed struggling in the water, and the craft floating down the river. An alarm was rinsed ; hut before assistance could be rendered both men :had disappeared and were drowned. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—At eight o'clock on Thursday morning the passenger train from Londonderry to Belfast narrowly escaped being precipitated into the River Bann. A number of the carriages left the line, and had the train not been stopped with the greatest promptitude it must have fallen into the river. Fortunately no damage was done, but the passengers were much shaken. The line was blocked for the greater part of the day. MR. GLADSTONE AND MITCHELSTOWN.—In a letter to the Secretary of the Chelsea Liberal Association, Mr. Gladstone Says it is difficult to overrate the evil effect which the laudatory acquittal pronounced by the Government on the Mitchelstown police is likely to produce on the proceedings of the Irish constabulary in every local case, such as may occur from day to day. If the people of England approved such an acquittal upon such a case as is before us, they would be unworthy the liberties which they themselves en- joy. AN EVICTION STRUGGLE: ONE MAN KILLED.—A tele- gram from Arklow reports that on Wednesday a large body of emergency men presented themselves at the house of Michael Kavanagh, of Croogham, caretaker of a farm pur- chased by Mr. John Kelly in the interest of the tenant, and seized several bead of cattle, but several people assembling they relinquished the stock. Shortly afterwards the emer- gency men were reinforced, the total force amounting to about 20 men all armed with rides, but were again beaten back. They they fired a volley of revolver and rifle shots, one of which took fatal effect, John Kinsella, a member of the resisting party, being stretched lifeless on the ground. Kinsella was over 60 years of age, and last July was evicted from his bolding on the Brooks estate. Several others re- ceived' shots, but without serious injury.
At Tiptre, Essex, Mr. Wallis has let a number ui allot- ments, ranging from two to 16 acres, at a rental of 30s. per acre. The labourers intend growing fruit.

The Prince of Wales visited Aldershot on Saturday, and presented new colours to the Ist battalion of the Norfolk Regiment, now under orders for Malta. The late Mr. David G. Hewitt, leather merchant, Edin- burgh and London, has left about £lOO,OOO for distribu- tion among charitable and benevolent institutions In Edinburgh and elsewhere. WHISKY CRISIS IN SCOTLAND.—Owing to the recent collapse of the firm of Kidd, Eunson, and ,Co., Leith, foui other firms in the whisky trade have bedn compelled to call meetings of their creditors. SUICIDE BY a MADMAN.—On Saturday, Daniel Joseph Ryan, who had been lately in an asylum, shot himself in his wife's presence in a house in Charlotte-street, Glas- gow. He died instantaneously. The Bishop of Rochester has requested the Dean not to complete his resignation till his return from America, but Dr. Scott is so seriously ill at the Deanery that the greatest fears are entertained for his life. • - • •• •

The committee of the Plymouth Mechanics' Institute upplied to the borough magistrates on Monday for a re- newal of their theatrical license; but it was refused on the ground that the means of escape were not sufficient To the manufacture of jam in East Kent is now to be added, as another expedient for relieving the agricultural depression, the manufacture of pickles, tons of which will be turned out from one factory alone in the course of a few weeks. _ .

„ While an old man was crossing the railway at Barrhead Station, near Glasgow, on Monday morning, he was caught by the London express and literally cut to pieces. The remains which could be found were collected and laid aside to await examination.

Mr. Goschen's Jubilee sixpences are selling freely in London at 2s. 3d. In shop windows where these coins are exposed for sale a gilded sixpence and a half-sovereign are exhibited on the same card, with the question, "Which is which ?" superadded. Whilst a detachment from the Channel Squadron were going through field exercise at Kirkwall on Monday, a field-piece fell upon a sailor from the Minotaur. breaking his leg. Another field-piece fell upon a sailor from the Monarch; the sufferers weretaken to the hospital. Another shocking case of burning, resulting from an attempt to blow out a paraffin lamp, has occurred in Liverpool. John Finn lies in the Northern Hospital in a critical condition. He was blowing down a lamp on iimaday evening, when he, was set on fire and so terribly burnt about the head and shoulders that it is doubtful if .ba will recover. _

An interesting archmological discovery has just been ' made between Canterbury 'and Folkestone. Some nay- vies, while excavating for the Elham Valley Railway, near Bridge, came upon an almost perfect circular well built of flint, which, it is stated, is undoubtedly Roman, and is but the opening of a subterranean passage leading under the old Butts. _

1 Early on Monday morning a man named Thorna.s Dean, 55, a provision dealer, of Bradshawgate, Leigh, com- mitted suicide in a shocking manner by shooting him- self through the head with a pistol. Deceased's house- keeper, at 5 40, heard a pistol-shot in an adjoining foom, I and, receiving no answer from her knock at the door, fetched a local doctor, who discovered the deceased in a pool of blood, dead. I Mr. Ellaway, formerly an alderman in the Birmingham 113Wn Council, was preaching on Sunday night nt the Circus Chapel, Bradford-street, and was just concluding 1 his discourse when he staggered forward in the pulpit and fell heavily. Some of the congregation rushed to his assistance. He was taken home Sri a cab unconscious, never rallied, and died about a couple of hours after- wards. The deceased gentleman was suffering from i heart disease.

-i-le-t-t-e-r—ii•om Lord Wolseley was read at a meeting held in Leeds on Monday to form a branch of the :National Association for employing army reserve men ' and discharged soldiers. His Lordship wrote in very flattering terms of the fitness of these men for civil em- ployment, and sought to remove the impression existing amongst employers of labour that they might be sud- denly and frequently deprived of their servants' assist- ance by a call to the colours.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A HIISRIND.—AIice Sheridan , died in Bootle Hospital on Monday morning from the result of injuries alleged to have been inflicted by her 'husband, who, it is stated, has been in the habit of ill- I using her for years. Last week he is alleged to have Iknociced her down and kicked her so violently that she was removed to the hospital, with the result stated. The woman's depositions were taken on Saturday. Her I husband went to sea on Saturday. A DEFAULTING BUILDING BDCIRTY.—Another of the Swansea building societies, termed the Co-operative, has 'Come to grief. It having accepted loans to the amount of £4,800 at Utile Olen the society had exceeded its borrowing powers, the solicitors have given notice to the lenders that the sociOy cannot legally pay the in- terest thereon or repay the principal. The depositor have already served writs on several directors, who are !respectable tradesmen in the town.

I Pocket-picking is particularly rife just now in London. I Wherever people congregate in any number there the ; light-fingered gentry are at work, and numerous com- plaints have been made of watches being stolen. The ' method most in vogue is to deftly draw the watch out , of the pocket, wrench it off the ring connecting it with the chain, and leave the latter ,dangling. It is known to Ithe police that juveniles are trained as pickpockets in as mrstematic a fashion as that described in "Oliver ITwist." ' DISSAPPOINTEIi ttiiril AND Spie/DE.—Another of thoee ' extraordinary suiciciel thiaugh what is called a love ' affair has just been discovered at Bowden, in T.eicester- shire. It appears that Miss Julia kid," aged TlZ,it I farmer's daughter, visited Leicester the CANT day, and e wrote home saying that in consecinenee ot a love affair I she would "be no more" when they received the letter. After being missing for 12 days her lifeless body has now been found in the canal, with the portrait of her sweetheart on her bosom. • On the arrival of the Cruion liner Wisconsin at Queens- town, on Saturday, it was reported that a gentleman, named Den worthy, aged 25, had committed suicide on the previous Sunday by jumping overboard. A lifebuoy was thrown to him and fell so close that it struck him, but he swam away from it. The engines were stopped, and the Wisconsin cruised round the spot for an hour and a half, but no trace of the man could be seen. Mr. IDenworthy had a brother on board, and was conversing ' with him only a minute before he sprang overboard.

Among the applicants to the magistrate at the Green- wich Police Court, on Saturday, WES a woman who !stated that she had had two husbands, both of whom were the sons of one mother, but not of the same fattier, The first husband died four years ago, and she had married the second eighteen months since, lie would not now support her, and she asked advice as to the legaliq of her marriage, and wished to know what to do. Mr. Sluel said the question was a conundrum which he could not answer. The law did not allow her to marry two brothers. The applicant had better throw herself on the parish, and they would seethe ease settled for her. A VALUABLE PATIENT.—The late Mr. Samuel J. Tilden, once Presidential candidate in the United States, was a ,'very rich man, and when his name was dragged Into an election mdvement piquant insinuations were certain about the traditional barrel of money be supplied. During the later years of his very long life Mr. Tilden was attended daily by Dr. Charles Simmons, and a doctor's bill containing 2,9oochargesfordaily attendance Is necessarily a long one, requiring an accountant to add up correctly. Frequently a rich man leaves something handsome to the physician who has kept him hopeful and cheerful in old age, but Mr. Tilden departed this life perhaps of the opinion that his doctor had earned a great reputation by attending so distinguished a man. Dr. Simmons, however, has his own Views on that point, and has brought an action to recover 143,000 dollars for pro- fessional services. A doctor who earns £3,500 &year out of one patient is in good practice. -

'ms 11YDROPEOBOI SCARR—There have recently been several deaths from hydrophobia in Liverpool and the surrounding district, and strict measures are being taken by the police in regard to seizing and destroying stray dogs. At an inquest on Monday on the body of a gardener at Roby who had died from this terrible dis- ease, the Coroner referred to the necessity of combined action being taken in every county division, as it was useless to muzzle dogs in one district and leave them free in another. Hydrophobia could be stamped out if a general order were enforced throughout the entire county. Tho Altrineham magistrates on Monday re- newed the dogs order for three months, on the applica- tion of a superintendent of police. A solicitor who was in court mentioned that there was quite a scare amongst the people of Sale and Asnton-on-Mersey, who by reason of the existence of rabies were almost afraid of sending their children to school. No fewer than 54 owners of dogs were summoned before the county magistrates, at Liverpool, yesterday, for allowing their animals to be at large, contrary to the order issued by the Bench last month, and were fined ss. and costs each, the aggregate amount of the penalties being £33 15s. The operation of the order was extended to the 31st October. THE POPE'S JUBILEE! A PREVENT APPLUL. A pastoral letter by Cardinal Manning was read on Sunday in the Roman Catholic churches of London. It pointed out that in June the English prelates invited the faithful to make ready their offerings to the Pope for the jubilee of his priesthood, which falls due on the last day of December, and that the deputation will be re- ceived by the Holy Father on Jan. 10 next. After statinr, that it would be a mortification and a humiliation if the offering were not worthy of the metropolitan diocese, the Cardinal proceeded;—" We have already told you that the needs of the Holy See are most urgent. It has been spoiled and stripped of all its possessions, and of all its ancient revenues. They who took away all that it possessed offered to give to the Sovereign Pontiff a civil fist, or an annual grant of public money, which the Vicar of Christ can receive from no man. He can never be the stipendiary of any civil Government, or dependent on Parliament or princes. From the day when the faithful laid their money at the Apostles' feet, the Church has depended upon the providence of God and the free-will offerings of the Christian world. These kilts became its patrimony, which is held by its own right; the highest and most sacred right of property upon earth. These rights have been violated, and the BolVneme can live in poverty, but it cannot sell its hide- r=

BREACH or TEE PEACE —Thomas Daley was summoned for having caused a disturbance by fighting in Buckley- street; he was dismissed.

ILL-TREATING A BORSE.—Thomas Knox, driver, and James Taylor, stableman, in the enmloy of the Warrington Carriage Company, were summoned by Inspector Spinks for causing a horse to be ill-treated en the 20th inst. It ap- peared that thettorse had slipped and fallen in Buttermarket- street, on the date mentioned, and on Inspector Spinks ex- amining the animal be found it suffering from a sore under- neath the saddle.—Mr. Collier, the manager of the com- pany, stated that stablemen had imperative orders net to allow any horse out which was suffering from a sore.—As Knox had only taken over the custody of the horse a few minutes before it fell, be was discharged; and Taylor was fined 5s and costs.

SLANDERING A CoNsTerum—James Forster, a butcher, residing in Eldon-street. was summoned for assaulting his wife on Sunday night, the 18th inst.—Constable Evans proved the cise.—De!endant declared that Constable Evans was drunk at the time, and that he violently ill-used him Inspector Cox and Sergeant Cheney haying been sent for, they deposed that they had seen Constable Evans both im- mediately before and after he had been at Forster's house, and he was perkctly sober.---The Bench ordered defendant to enter into two sureties of £2O each to keep the peace for six months, or in default to be imprisoned fer one month.

BEGGING.—Thomas Kelly, for begging in Manchester- road,on the afternoon previous, was sent to prison for seven days. DrerrnsEnsinss.—James Sauce, charged with having been drunk and disorderhy in Irlam-street, on the previous night, was fined 5s and costs, and Sarah Burke, for having been drunk and disorderly in Hill-street, was fined 5.3 including costs.

The magistrates fined him 5s and costs, and directed that he should pay for the damage done. In default he must go to prison for a fort. night.

Barber wee charged with having removed three pigs from Warrington lot , Cheshire contrary to the orders of the local authority. Defendant pleaded guilty, but said he had I not been aware that he was committmg any offence. The :chairman (Mr. E. Greenall) said it was a great pity the Corporation of' Warrington did not work with the two counties. The defendant thought a notice should be put up , in the market. The Chairman assented, bat said that the bench bad no power to order such a notice to be put up. There were couflicting interests; the Corporation of War- rington got a rent from the pig market. The defendant said that tbe pig dealers did not care who they sold to as long as they did sell. The Chairman: That is it.—A fine of ss. I and costs was imposed. SUNDAY DRINKING.— Frederick Chaplin, landlord of the Ram's Heed Inn, Grappenhall, was summoned for hay- ing on Sunday, the 4th September, kept his licensed 1 premises open at a time Ween be wee required by the law to keep it cies/A, hardily, ai half-past 11 ocilock. The follow- ing persons were charged with having been on the premises of the Ram's Head on the occasion referred to, viz.:— Frederick Clark, 121, Mersey-street; Thomas Sloane, 44, Hopwood-street; Joseph Smith, 4, Admiral-street; Frederick Whittaker, White Bull Hotel, Horsemarket• street ; Henry Nich0111: Hereereareet•street; James Slater, 10, Howley- lane ; James Backbones, 19, Greenall-street ; Thomas IKennon, 63, Ellesmere-street ; lobs Haelam, 40, General- , Street; John Holmes, 11, Greenall-street ' • and Wm. Davies, 1 11, Tanners-lase. Mr. F. Browne, eollcitor, Warrington. , appeared on behalf of Chaplin. In giving evidence for the prosecution, Sergeant Boeth stated that on the morning of the 4th inst., at 11-30 o'clock be, in company with P.C. Bennett, went to the Ram's Head Inn. lee knocked at the front door, and after some delay he was admitted. On entering the taproom he there found some of the defendants. He called the landlord's attention to their presence, and asked what they were doing there. The lanalord replied that they were all travellers. He (witness) then asked the men for their names and addresses. He also found the other defendants In the parloar, and the landlord said they were also travellers. He had since found that the whole of the meh, apart from Chaplin, lived at Warrington, and within three milet of the Raft/ nead,—P.C. Mr. Browne after- wards addressed the court on behalf of his client, and a number of witnesses were called in defence. The Bench, however, decided to fine Frederick Chaplin in the sum of 408 and costs (the conviction not to be endorsed on the license.) The charges against Clarke, Sloan, Whittaker, and Nicholls were dismissed, and the other defendants were fined in the sum of Is each and costs.—Mr. Brewne gave notice of appeal in the case of Mr. Chaplin. div.head: HARVEST FiSTIVALS. BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: HARVEST FiSTIVALS. BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.

The harvest festival in connection with Bewsey- road Wesleyan Chapel was celebrated on Sunday. when a sermon was preached in the morning by the Rev. T. Baine, of St. Helens, and in the evening by the Rev. E. 11. Jackson, of Warrington. At each service there was a large congregation, and in the evening, in particular, the large edifice was was thoroughly filled. The decoration of the in- terior of the chapel had been carried out in a very complete and tasteful fashion. The front of the pulpit, while not hidden behind an indiscriminate collection of produce, was yet most handsomely and appropriately embellished with vegetables, cereals, fruits, and flowers. The decoration of the other parts of the chapel—the pillars, gas brackets, and windows—harmonised admirably with that of the pulpit. The pillars were wreathed with corn, interspersed with various coloured flowers, the gas brackets were similarly adorned, and the windows ' were inlaid with judiciously assorted masses of the products of the fi-.ld and garden. Each of the gal- lery panels was hung with its chaplet of flowers, e,ars of corn, or fruit, while the partition in front of the choir gallery. was also lavishly decorated, the motto "The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof," being to some extent concealed behind graceful festoons. Those to whom the credit of the decorations is mainly due are Mrs Swift, Miss , Swift, Mrs I. Hay Ward, Misses Horton, Misses Jones, Miss Beaman' Mr. John Swift; Mr. A. H. Dunn, and Mr. E. Dallow. Mr. W. J. Horton and his family deserve special mention for their share of the work. At the evening service an anthem was excellently sung by the choir, Miss L. Horton rendering a' solo part with fine effect. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

I The harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday at Warrington Parish Church, and each service was largely attended. In the morning the sermon was preached by the Ilev. D. Ellison, rector of All Saints, Manchester. The prayers were rend by the Revs. J. A. Drummond and T. IL Twist, and the lessons by the. Rev. E. j. Wilcock's, while the communion service Was taken by the Rev. J. A. Drummond and J. J. Langham. The words of the anthem were taken from the 145th Psalm, "All thy works praise thee," the music being by Mr. T. M. Pattison. The solo was well rendered by lb. R. T. Fairclough, and Mr. W. S. Woods presided at the I organ. The preacher selected as the subject of his I discourse Dent. xvi. 13 and 14. The preacher in the ; afternoon' was the Rev. J. A. Drummond. Appro- priate hymns were sung, Dr. Green's anthem, "Thou jvisitest the earth," being well rendered. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. A. 'Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn. Every seat was occupied at six o'clock. half an hour before the I time appointed for the service to commence. • The ; chancel was also tilled, as well as a number of form 4 Iwhich Were placed in the aisles. The Faytt's Were read by the Rev. T. 11. Twists end the lessons by the !Rev. E. .1, Willcocks. The words of the anthem were taken from the 59th Psalm and part of the 16th verse—" I will sing of thy power." The solo was again taken by Mr. Fairclough. The words of the text were from Deut. xxvi. 10. The interior of the church, it is needless to say, was very elaborately decorated in the customary manner. The fob o rang is a list of the pm- ' j elptil &Coition :—Communion and chancel, the clergy daughters, under the superintendence of Miss ' Beale; choir stalls, the Mime Chritnes and Brooke; clergy stalls, the Misses itobinedn ; prayer desk, the !Misses Dooley; pulpit, the Misses Allen; south win- dows, Miss Boyle; font, Mrs. Quekett ; and gaseliers, Miss Cassidy, Miss Taylor, and others. Grapes and flowers were contributed to the decorators by kind friends, friends, and a large supply of wheat and corn, was sent by various farmers. Other contribu- tors were as follo'ces :—Flower; the Mayoress. Alderman Crosfield, Mr, Peter Stubs, lir. Chidlaw, pthe Rector (gladioli from Somersetshire), Mr. Win. Brookes, Mrs. Francomb, Mrs. William Woods ; fruit, Mr. and Mrs. Walton and Mr. and Mrs. Dew- hurst ; vegetables, Mr. Meredith. Mr. Pierpoint, three beautiful sprays of pampas grass; Mr. Samuel 'Davies, a large loaf and six small bags of four. We were pleased to notice the tablet to the memory Of the late Mr. Eaude had also been remem- bered. It bore a wreath composed of choice white flowers, with a border of beautiful white asters, the gift of Mrs. Cawley and Mr. P. Pearse. The work of decoration, which had been entrusted to Miss Ada Chrimes, was most chaste:' CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE. The annual harvest festival in connection with Christ Church, Padgate, was held on Sunday, and the services, both morning and evening, were largely attended. The church was handsomely decorated. The ladies who did the work of decoration were —Mrs Williams, the Misses Turner, Miss Sansom, the Misses Woods, and Miss Antrobus. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton conducted the morning service, and also preached. At evening service the Rev. I. Phillips, of Orford, read the prayers, while the Rey. W. H. Williams, vicar of Padgate, intoned the ser- vice and preached. The offertory (which was in aid of the organ fund) was then taken up. the amount received at morning and evening service, together with donations, exceeding £l6. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, LYMbi.

The annual harvest festival of the above place of worship was held on Sunday. The preacher at both morning and evening 'services was the Rev. David Pawson, of Didsbury College. The anthemr" The earth is the Lord's," was sung by the choir at the evening service. The church was very tastefully decorated, the windows, communion 'table, pulpit, galleries, and gas standards having special care bestowed upon them. The following ladies and gentlemen helped materially in the decoration of the church :—Mrs. Dodds, Miss A. Brown, and Mr. D. Brown, the pulpit and communion table; the Misses Jones, the gallery; Mrs. A. Mairs, Mrs. F. 0. Moston Misses Hazeldine, Moston, Pickton (2), Bate, Leigh, and Mr. A. Mairs. The Misses Machlin, Mrs. Child, and Messrs. E. Moston, W. B. Moston, J. Harrington, E. Cliff, James Malts, T. 3fairs,.Brockle- burst, and Wilkinson also helped generally. Mr. F. 0. Moston was responsible for the decoration of the chandeliers and gas standards. Thanks are due to Mr. Benjamin Parr for moss for the windows, and to Messrs. Dodds, J. Mairs, and T. Mairs for the loan of .plants. The Misses Jones and Messrs. Wilkinson and Winstanley also assisted by sending corn and flowers. The collections were for general circuit

_— expenses. During the week harvest thanksgiving services have also been held a St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, and St. Anne's and St. Barnabas', Warring- ton, and at each place the services were largely at- tended.
Aldermso De IC-ysev was on Thursday elected Lord Maya of London for the year commencing on the 9th ot November.

Lord Wolselev unveiled at Handley, on Thureday morn- ing, a monument te Lord St. Vincent, who died of wounds received at the battle of Abu Klea, in the Soudan. At Doncaster, on Thursdny, Taylor, the driver. and Daviea, the fireman of the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lin- colnshire train in the Llexthorpe accident, were again re- manded on bail.

Loss OF A SHIFLDS ,STEAMER AND TEN LIVES. On Wednesday night a ielegrani was received in South Shields from Vigo by Hall, Cay. and Co. manazing owners of the screw steamer Marl new Can of South Shields, announcing that that vessel struck the reeks off Finisterre and sank im- mediately. Nme of the crew were saved and ten were drowned. The 11011,8 of the nun drowned are at present unknown. lhe steamer was bound from Troon to Genoa and was commandtd by Captain William Thomas, of South Shields. Several of the crew belong to South Shields. Great anxiety preveils respecting the wreck, as news can- not be obtained for several days. The steamer was 1,350 toss register.

If, on the other hand, he allows Irish representation in the English Parliament to continue as heretofore, the grave difficulty presents itself that Irishmen will be able to direct not only their own affairs, but, to a large extent, the affairs of this country. Those who are opposed to Home Rule in any form press both of these objec- tions as they have a perfect right to do. For our own part, we acknowledge the full force of these considerations; but for all that we should like to see the experiment tried of giving Home Rule to Ireland and permitting representation in England ; because, in the first place, it least divides the Liberal party, and because, in the second place, it will sooner lead to the right remedy for all these difficulties—namely, Home Rule all round. Let the people of England, and Scotland, and Wales once perceive that Ireland has an advantage over them in having the autho- rity to manage her own affairs, and they will ' soon see the necessity of each having simi- lar powers—particularly when they find that Ireland has power, too, to stop the working 'of their own cumbersome machinery. div.p: In preparing the above, we have been guided in the main by the official statement of ac- counts last published With regard to the income, we may say that the actual total of fines for last year was £l9 4.s Bd. It is not too much to assume that the receipts from this source would be more than doubled when the readers were quadrupled. Those who have so little faith in our working popu- lation will probably say that the income from "lost and damaged books" would be more than .4.s 9d, but we have taken the figures as last year, and so also with regard to the receipts from " sale of catalogues," " advertisements in catalogues," " sale , of periodicals," and "hire of chairs " In- stead of ios for " bile of lecture room," we have put down £ to. Mr. Morixs J.P., offered to give that sum for its use for a year ; but if it were put in the market the income would probably be still greater. Turning to the expenditure side, we have taken salaries at £236 19s 6d, the total for 1886 and the average of the past four years. Considering the ex- cellentcondition in which the Museum has been placed by the recent large outlay, £ro per year would cover its requirements for several years to come. Last year the sum expen- ded in this department was £35 os 9d, but it included unusual items, consequent on the recent alterations. The Art Gallery expenses last year were Er+ ss 6d, and for the year previous they came to Et r 17 3d. The re- duction ta £9 i7s 6d is therefore trifling. In the Library Department the expenditure for last year is £l9B tzs 6d, but this in- cludes £79 los for catalogues, and will not occur again for some years. It brings the total down to Li 19 23 61, and this we have reduced to £75. allowing, say, £4.0 for now books, &c., and £35 for wear and teat. Coming to the "establishment expenses— other than salaries," we have struck out the following items, which will not occur again for a while, being the outcome of the altera- tions :—" Thos. Hesketh and Sons, painting, colouring, &c., £127." "Joseph Moun- field. altering book cases, £BB izs 9d," and S. E and R. Johnson, linoleum. £zB tos." This still leaves £195 izs 3d a year for " es• tablishment expense;," tht amount we have put down, a sum fully sufficient under oidi- nary circumstances, as it is LIZ more than the total for the previous year. Those figures show, it will be perceived, a small balance on the right side. They show also what can be done without a penny in the way of sub- scriptions, and are an effectual answer to those who, without taking the trouble to in- vestigate the matter, are too ready to say that the Library and Museum cannot be maintained without the aid of a subscrip- tion which proves to be an infraction of the law, and a gross injustice to the inhabi- tants.

SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN —A shocking sudden death occurred at Runcorn on Thursday afternoon. John Raw- son, about fifty years of age, a bachelor, who resided in Newtown, was on his way to consult Dr. Robinson, when he entered the yard of Mr. Nichols, Queen.street. Me had been there but a brief time, when be fell to the ground, and vomited blood in large quantities. Dr. Robinson, who Was quickly in attendance, ordered his removal to his sister's home, where he expired in a few seconds. We understand the doctor has given a certificate of the cause of death. NARROW ESCAPE AT WIDNES.—Dn Thursday, a girl, about 17 years of age, named Myers, living at 6, Mary. street, Moss-bank, Widnes, bad a narrow escape from being crushed to death. The girl was nursing a young baby, and somehow or other she became jammed botween a wall and a cart heavily laden with a number of pigs. On seeing what was about to happen, she thoughtfully let the child fall out of her arms on to the ground, and it escaped without in- jury. The girl, however, had her shoulder bone broken, besides receiving other injuries Dr. Burgess was summoned and attended to the girl, who is yet in a serious condition. The weather was all the could be desired. The re- turn journey was made at 7-15 pro., all having thoroughly enjoyed the autumn afternoon in the country. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.—On Monday at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Henry White, a carter in the em- ploy of Mr. Johnson of Nerthwich, pleaded guilty to a charge of cruelly illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. Sergeant Oldfield deposed that on the 21st September, he saw the defendant driving a brown lime which was attached to a cart laden with bricks. He discov- ered that the animal was suffering from two wounds under the collar, each being about two inches wide and four inches long. Defendant admitted that he knew the animal was suffering from the wounds bat he was compelled to work it. The Sergeant said the horse was suffering great p tin —Thal defendant now said that the horse had been standing in the stable for ten 'lays previous to the day on which it Wee worked. The animal had a beat lump under its collar, and thie became a sore.—The Bench considered the casa a very bad one. and fined the defendant 20s and coets 16s.

Hnsband, the deputy coroner, en Saturday held an inquest at the Prince , of Wales Hotel, Kent-street, Widnes, touching the death of John Howard, who was a labourer at the Thareis copper works, and lives at 38, Appleton Village. It appeared that Howard, who was 48 years of age, lost his wife in February last, and hie manner had since been very strange, and he had ! been much addicted to drinking. When he ariived home on Wednesday night his Sister, Ellen Devenport. a widow,l Pulled his boots off. Deceased told her that he should not want the boots any more, and asked her to throw them be- hind the fire. She declined, and then he asked her to cut his head off. He bad had some drink. Afterwards be went to bed, and during the night his sister beard him vomiting. About six o'clock next morning she heard him moaning, and when she got down stairs, two boors later, she fornd him in the kitchen hanging by the neck from a rope fixed to a beam. He was quite dead. A verdict of suicide whilst temporarily insane was returned. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT WIDNES PARISI( CHURCH:- Services of thanka4ivine for the harvest have been held in St. Mary's Parish Church. It is curious to observe how certain miners will violate the provisions of the Coal Mines Regulation Act, which has been passed in theft interest. At the Newton Petty Sessions, On Saturday, Thomas Clarke was fined 20S and costs for UnrAmrning A shot that had failed to fire. Ile knew that in doing this he was risking his own life and the lives of others, and fully merited the penalty which was in- flcted upon him.

Mr. W. Murphy, M.P., is repotted to have said, at a meeting of the National League in Dublin, on Tuesday, that the murder of Head-constable Whelehan had the appear- ance of a put up job. We feel bound to pro- test against language of this Rind. It can serve no good purposes to suggest that the authorities—cruel as they are—would sacrifice the life of one of their own officers to create a feeling against the National League.

It is very hard for Irishmen to have to lis- ten while patience is being preached, when at the same time they are denied the right of open assembly and free speech. Still, every outrage, whatever the provocation, tells against their cause. The Government can- not, of course, suppress the League so long as the people are willing to stand by th eir principles at the risk of having to go to gaol. O'Connell said it was impossible to frame an indictment against a whole nation ; and it is certainly impossible to put a whole nation in prison.

The Yankees are always inventing some good thing. The latest outcome of their genius is a dynamite gun, which is said to be capable of destroying the strongest ironclad. If this be so, it will be no use building iron- clads, and a great deal of money will oe saved. Better still, if this gun prove so des- tructive, and become the common property of the civilised world, there will be less dis- position to go to war, and the world will be more at peace. "There is a soul of good in things evil."

An elephant travelling with a circus es- caped from its stable, at Rugby, on Monday, and went "on the spree." The lively brute entered a cottage, and, unfastening the cup- board, ate a dozen pots of jam, a gallon Qt pickled onions, a quantity of damsons, a joint of meat, a loaf of bread, a ponnri of butter, and a quantity of sweets, finishing up with browsing the window plants. It then placed all the 'chimney ornaments on the sofa, and enjoyed itself for two hours before being got out. The elephant's trunk is like many another trunk—it is the receptacle for very many curious things.

The Rev. E. Hodgson, vicar of Shock. lock, Cheshire, is at loggerheads with his parishioners on account of his high church practices. He was provided with a hassock, h2sing stated that there was none; but it would seem that he had singular notions as to its use, for it is alleged that he took it from the table and jumped on it. In re- turn some of the parishioners would like to jump on the vicar. "The quarrel is a very pretty quarrel as it stands." When the Church is separated from the State, there will be less nonsense of this kind; the clergy will have more regard for the wishes of their congregations.

On Monday six boys were brought before the magistrates, at Runcorn, for playing at whip top on the public footpath. They were ordered to pay 3s 6d each as costs. No doubt an offence was committed, and the magis trates are bound to deal with such cases when they are brought before them. But, as Mr. John Morley said the other day, there is such a thing as common sense in administering the law; and it is net being exercised when lads are summoned for playing whip top. " All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy." The curmudgeon who does not care to step aside when a boy is whipping his top on the footpath deserves to be whipped himself.

THE MEMBER FOR NEWTON AND Me RECENT CAPTURE.—A letter has been received this week by Mr. and Mrs. Legh, of Lyme Hall, Disley, from their son, Mr. Thomas Wodehouse Legh, M.P., under date of Sofia, in which he states in a jocular manner, "that he has proved too much for once for the brigands in that quarter," but does not give any details of his capture and release by them. Mr. Wyndham, the British Minister to Servia, has been staying at Lyme Hall, and left there on Tuesday. He was astonished that Mr. Legh escaped so easily from the brigands. Slur CANAL COMPANY.— The Ship Canal Com- pany's tug boats have been towing their vessels up the river this week, in consequence of the scarcity of water in the Bridgewater Canal, owing to the dry weather. It will behove the directors to see to a fresh supply for summer consumption while the Ship Canal is in course of construction. No doubt Mr. Williams will see to such an important matter, and will be able to keep the traffic in regular pro- gress. On Thursday Mr. Walker, contractor of the Ship Canal works, paid a visit to Barton, and, after taking several measurements, proceeded to Irlam, and from thence to Warrington. He had with him the plans of the proposed works.

WIDNES COLINTY COURT.—A sitting of this court was held yesterday tw His Hononr Judge Collier. The cause list comprised 120 plaints and 50 judgment summonses.— , Mark Steinhart jeweller, of Manchester, brought au action against James Chesworth, carter, Liverpool, to recover £4 17s 64, balance of account for the sale of a watch. Mr. George Rideal, solicitor. Warrington. was for the olaintiff The watch was sold in November, 1879, the price being fixed at £6 10s. Since then the defendant bad made various payments, reducing the amount owing to the sum sued for.—The defendant alleged that he had completely linnidated the debt, and produced a receipt dated July 18. h, 1880. The stamp used, however, was of a kind which Was not issued by the postal authorities until June, 1881. Mr. Steinhart also denied on oath that the signature was his.— His Honour gave judgment against the defendant, and impounded the receipt he had produced. To HIRE SYSTEM AT WIDNES —At 'Widnes County Court, yesterday, befor His Honour Judge Collier, Messrs Toaster and Co.. of Liverpool. sued Thomas Platt, labourer at the works of Messrs Mathieson. and who resided in Waterloo-road, to recover £1 for the hire of a wringing machine. Mr. Lewin was for the defendant. Mr. Towler appeared in person, and alleged that a wringing m +chine, worth £2, was supplied, but an old machine was taken as part payment. A man named William Evans was celled to prove that the signature on the agreement for the hire was that of the defendant, but instead of doing AO, Evans Paid he must tell the truth, and stated that Pla't was not present when the agreement was drawn np.—The defendant said the machine was brought to the hone., In his absence. and the old one taken away. When he discovered this he wanted to throw the machine inm the Street. He never knew anything shout the agreement until his wife's death in August—Judgment was given for the defendant with costs.

RABIES IN WIDNES Dtvistow.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday. Ssperintendent Johnston applied for an order that all dogs in the Widnes T ivision should be either confined or kept under control. The Superintendebt reid letter showing that there was groat suspicion of canine madness existing in the division to a considerable extent, and he added that rabies were very prevalent in the out- skirts of the division. A. dog /inspected of being mad had bitten a number of dogs in Widnes, and bad been bnt. The carcase of the animal was lying in the police court yard awaiting a prod mortem examination. A dog had also been shot at Hallwood ; but. in this instance neither animate nor human beings had been bitten.—Mr. H. G :s- -teel% sen., said the coneeqnences of the bite of a tnad dog were so terrible that the Bench under the circumstances thought that they mast acquiesce is the superintendent's application —The Bench then granted a general order to date from October let to December 31st. The townships included are Widnes, Bold, Crouton, Ditton, Hale, Hale- wood, Rainhill, and Speke. BOYS AND THEIR WHIP TOPS AT" RUNCORN —At Ran. corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Rey- nolds and Mr. James Handley. six lads named William Dwyer, John 'Jones. .Tohn Glover. Arthur Ellis, James Bushels, and Joseph Plant, were each summoned for play- ing whip too on the footpath in the public streets.—Suner- intendent Hollingworth said this was an action the police did not like to take, bat the complaints with regard to stone throwing and whip top had been so numerous from every part of the town that the police were obliged to take some steps In endeavour to put the practice down. The police , did not ask for revere punishment, hut they wished to shim that thee,. were offences to the annoyance and danger of the public,and could sot be carried on with impunity.—P.C.Kettle and constables 252 and 149 proved the cases.—Mr.Reynolds raid this thing roust be stepped, and each defendant would have to pay costs, Sc Gl—Mr. Dwyer, father of one of the ' defendants. asked if it would, not have been as well if the constables had taken the whips and then given the boys a switch with them. The parents had as much as they could do to find school money for the htoys.---Supsrintendent Hal- liogworth said the parents would be the first to take ACl'nll against the police if a stick had been used.—Mr. Reynolds : The parents are the people to use the stick.—Superintend- ent Hollingworth : People coma here and ask the police far protection, and they were obliged to give it them.—The parents then paid the money.--Joseph Plant, eight years of age, pleaded guilty to throwing /genes in Church-street, th.. 21st ultimo, and he was ordered _to pay weds.

. • ODTIFFLLOWSHIP T HA.LTO`f —On Wednesday evening, the members of the 't 'Celine Sun" lodge. No. 628. of the Grand United Order of Otielfellowe, Halton and Runcorn District, met at their lodge room, Castle Hotel, Halton. for the purpose of presenting the trustees. Brothera Robert Huehes and Job Hancock, each with an illuminated em'elem of the Order. The President (Brother H Rowe, junior) occupied the chair. and Brother W Speakman the vice- chair, and amongst the officers and member present were— Brother Joseph Mnnnia, secretary ; Brothers R Hughee, Job Hancock, John M Bosworth, W H Thomaston, J Faulk- ner. H Clare. Thomas Potter, John Hazlehurst„Toseph Hor- ton, jun., Thomas Wilkinson, Henry Walker, Ire. The presentation was mede by Brother Joseph Manning. who said that for the laat few years the dutiee of the trustees had been very heavy, and taking this into consideration. and the smell remnneration they received, it had been re- -8 dyed to present Brothers Hughes and Hancock each with an emblem of the Order, and Brother Bosworth with a small remuneration in money. He referred to the faithful duties of the trustees, and said so long as the officers and members continued to work together in unity, so long would their prosperity increase. Brother Hughes, Brother Hancock, and Brother Bosworth responded in suitable terms. A hearty vote or thank.; was then accorded the secretary, and Brothers Faulkner and Thomson, for the interest they had taken in the &siren and preparation of the embleme; and vote or thanks to the chairman terminated a pleasant even- ing. The work of illumination was executed by Mr E J Reynolds, The Avenue, Manchester.
