Joseph Fat lion, 14 years ef age, whose house is I in Norib-strest,{7lB ch irged with stealing a shirt, value 2., the property of Hannah Jones, a widuw who lives at 9. Waterloo-road.—The prisoner was s.en to take the shirt from a clothes line, and as he had previously Ine..; before the magistrates, he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour, afteruauls to be confined in a reformatory school for four days.

WIDNES POLICE COCHT —Yesterday, before Mr. H. Gas- hell, junr., Thomas C4rr, about 17 years of age, was cliarr.,ed with Nutcooding from we training ship, akbar. Toe pri- soner iriv4 apprehended by &.rgeant Clarkson, and was re- manded to await the arrival of an officer to convey him to the vessel.--Catherine Carey, who is under police .super- -. .
vision at St. 11.1Pns, was ch.r.g.td with ben g in Widnes without reporting h•-rself. On the evidence et P.S. Robin- son be was remind:A until (tether inquiries could be made

A IteTZSTANI. THIEF AT WIDNES U R Incorn Police Court, on Thurslay. torture M. J. Brundrit and Mr. J. Handley, Thomas Harrison was coarged with stealing a purse containing Os 44, from a drawer in a dwelting- bongo at Norton, the proporty of Thom is Smiles. The prisoner and two other men, who are employed at Norton Waterworks, lodged with Mr Stokes. On the 19th Septem- ber the purse was missed from a drawer, and information was given to the police. Four drys liter the prisoner asked one of his fellow lodg.-rs to hand the purse and money to Mr, Skis with a reqii et for forgiveness.—The prisoner was now lined 40s, or a month's imprisonment. The money WNIR trail.

, MUNIFICENT GIFT BY MR. BRUNNER, M.P.—On Thursday, at a meeting of the Free Library Com- mittee at Winsford, a letter was received from Mr. Brunner, M.P., stating that it was his intention to send a cheque for £4OO towards the Free Library to be erected there in commemoration of Her Majesty's Jubilee. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Brun- ner for his generosity. SEVERE FROSTS IN CHEsumE.—Frosts have set in early and with unusual severity in Cheshire. On Thursday morning the ponds in exposed fields were frozen over with ice of considerable thickness. For several mornings past the country has been white with the frost rime. The cold weather is greatly retarding the pastures which were coming into excellent conditi in since the drought passed away.

CINAL BOATS As DwimiANGs.—John Ifeatlicote, the ina.:stvr of a canal boat, appeared at the Warring- ton Borough Court, on Monday, in answer to a sum- mons charging him with allowing his boat to be in an unclean condition, in consequence of which it was not fit for habitation, on Ow 51h September. The boat was examined when berthed at Bank Quay, and both the aft and fore cabins were found to be dirty. Defendant, who said that the cabins got wet in consequence of the deck being out of repair, was fined 203 and costs. _

. • HAYDOCK PARK COURSING MEETING.—The Lan- cashire coursing season openecl on Wednesday morning over the well-known and popular enclosure at Ilaydock Park, when a fairly excellent pro- gramme was discussed. The stakes scarcely filled so well as had been expected, but a very capital card of sixty-four courses provided ample sport to satisfy the most exacting of spectators. Several puppies of great promise were amongst the entries, the principal kennels of the country having sent representatives, and many exciting trials took place.

I ALARMING CARR/AGE ACCIDENT. A serious carriage accident occurred at Newton Bridge on Thursday. Dr. Heyward, of Haydock, with his wife and coachman, drove up to New- ton Bridge Station. The doctor having alighted and gone on to the platform, the horse Lom some cause shied. Turning sharply round, it upset the carriage, throwing out Mrs Hayward and the coach- man. The man was thrown with great force , against the wall, sustaining severe injuries. The doctor was soon in attendance, and the man was conveyed in an unconscious state into the Legh Arms Hotel, from which he was afterwards re- moved in an ambulance to the Cottage Hospital, Ilaydoek. Mrs Heyward fortunately received btlt little injury. The horse broke off both shafts of the carriage, and made off with fearful speed 'through Newton; but riventually it was stopped and ! brought back to the hotel. I Ism& OF MAN STEAMERS. The popularity and success of the Lancashire Witch has been so surpri- sing this year, that it is no wonder the New Isle of Man Steam Navigation Company are preparing to put more .boats on the station next season. As showing the enormous stimulus given to the Isle of , Man holiday traffic, we may state that in the three summer months of this year, 144,533 persons landed at Douglas against 77,454 in the corresponding period last year. There is every reason to believe that such leaps and bounds in the traffic are likely to continue, and if this is so, here will be plenty of work and profit for several more vessels of the Lan- cashire Witch Type—fast, economical, and containing the latest improvements in structure and machin- ery. It will be seen from our advertising columns that a further issue of £5 shares is now being offered, and the investment appears to us to be a really promising one. The offices of the company are at 15 and 19, Sweeting-st,Tet.
NORTHWICH PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION LICENSED VICTUALLERS' ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the immibers of this association was held on Wednesday afiernoon at the Rea Lion Hotel, Over. Mr. T. E. Skidmore, the president, eccupied the chair, and there 'vie a good attendance of members, a num- ber having driven from Ruecorn. The balance sheet, submitted by Mr. W. H. Hughes, the seeretary, showed re- ceipts, including £033 subscriptions frem members, amount- ing to £lO5 13s hi. After paying all expenses there was a balance in the bank of £4l 14s 101—In moving the adop- tion of the balance sheet. the Chairman pointed out that there were ten less members than last year, and there had been a proportionate falling off in the subscriptions. He appealed to those present to endeavour to increase the mern- bership.—Mr. Skidmore was re-eiected president, and Messra H. Coward (Runcorn), Themes Wood (Northwich), and James R4W802:1 Wineord), were appointed vice-presi- dent.. Mr. Wood was also appointed the treasurer, and Mr. W. H. Hughes was retained as secretary. Mr. Arthur Hough was appointed secretary for the Runcorn dietrlet, and Messrs S. Armstrong, J. J. Waterworth, sod H. Coward, were deputed to he a committee for the same district. It was resolved that the next annual meeting should be held at Rencorn. Subseqmently about sixty mem- bers and visitors eat down to dinner. The post of honorsr was occupied by the president, who was supported I by the following from Raucorn :—Messre. H. Coward, 3, J. I Waterwortb. S. Armstrong, A. Hough, W. Anderton„ W. Hankinsoo, George Turley, and I. Stubbs. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts having been given, the Chairman pro- posed the "Army, navy, and resPrve forces." to which Mr. , tfankinson appropriately responded.—Mr. Badger, chairman 1 of the Ceevre and Nontwich Ace 'el ition. proposed 'Success I to the Northwich Division Licensed Victuallers' Aesocia- Hon." He remarked that t here were a vast number of per- sons in the trade. who, wbile they had the benefit of the association's work and resources, took no interest in their claoa beyond drawing liquors. There had been cases in that division where innovation was attempted to be placed in the trade, and men wha had no right to expect such a thing had been protected. He thought it was the duty of every licensed victualler to support the association. (Applause.) —The Chairman responded. He observed that the poor publican had not been the subject of any legisla- tion during the past session, but there was no doubt that in the near feture there would be some new legislation, and they ought to be prepared to meet it not individually, bat collectively, by bringing pressure to bear upon the members of the House of Corn. ' moos. With regard to last year, four members of the asso- ciation had charges brought agaiest them, and they were all dismissed. (Applause.) He pointed out the advantages of the association, and urged those present to endeavour to increase the membership. He did hope Runcorn would put the shoulder to the wheel, and bring them some members. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by giving "The visitors," for whom Mr. Ashley, secretary of the Crewe Association, re- plied. He impressed upon the licens-d victuallers the im- portance of being unite I. Their enemies in the House of Commons were only waiting for an opportunity to pounce upon them, and their only object was to exterminate them. Their enemies looked upon mein as so many vermin, and it was only lea combination and cultivating a friendly spirit amongst themselves that they could counteract the influ- ence which their opponents bed undoubtedly obtained. (Ape please.) As aeon as poor Paddy was settled, the aggressive war would he carried on as before.—Other toasts were given, and the company were amused by recitations by Mr. G. Turley., and lamas by the chairman, Mr. Aatley, Mr. Brain, Mr. Whitehead, Mr. Peter Welker, Ai:.

MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT WIDNES. At Widnes P)lice Court, on Monday, bafore Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Michael Clarke, 40 years of age, a labourer, was brought up charged with having. on the 10th Senternher, maliciously wounded John Pet. trier, aged 45. The case bad been reminded on several occasions because rettner was unable to appear. rhe prosecutor, who is a bricainaker, and the prisoner are lodgers at the same house, No. 16, Nelson-street. About seven o'clock on the'evening of the 20th ult. the prosecutor heard the prisoner calling his son a thief and a rogue, and other foul names. At length the son appealed to his father, who asked the prisoner if he had sent the boy on an errand and he had kept some money as he had used such language. rhe prisoner replied that the boy had kept nothing, and again 053 d bad language. " Come, lat's have no such lan• guage as that," said the prosecutor, and suddenly the pri- soner rose from the &air upon which he had been sitting, and raising a cleaver aloft, struck the prosecutor a fright- ful blow on the head. He then aimed another blow at him, but his aim was diverted, and and the we•pon struck him slightly under the chin. The prosecutor became unconscious, and he was afterwards con- fined to bed for nine days. He was even now subject to pains in the head. The prosecutor informed the magistrates

that he had known the prisoner for six rn..nths, and daring that period had never had an angry word with him.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed that the prosecutor had suffered from an incised wound on the upper and left side uf the fore- head, extending towards the cream, The wound was an inch and three quarters in length, and penetrated to the bone. A portiom of the skull was exposed. He stitched the wound, which was a very, dangerous one. Had tho , cleaver been sharper it would have cleft the Ault. As it was, considerable violence must have been used tl cause such a wound as the prosecutor. suffered fronts—P.C. Wore- fold stated that when he went to the house on the night in question, the prisoner bad fastened himself in the kitchen, and he had to break open the door. The prisoner alleged that the prosecutor had struck him five or six times before he gave a blow. There were, be added, not ten words be- tween them togvther.—Tbe prisoner was committed to the Assizes fur trial.

A SHIPPING DISPUTE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. EL Gaskell, senr., and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Thomas Hadley was cbarged that he, being in possession of the certificate of registration of the flat Morning Star, did refuse to deliver the same up to Mr. John Medley, and the co-owners of the vessel, who were the persons entitled to the certificate for the lawful navigation of the flat.—Mr. Peters WAS for the complainants, and Mr. Thompson, of Liverpool, was for the defendant.—Mr. Gasketl expressed the opinion that a case of this descriprion, being a dispute between the owners of a vessel, ought to be settled by arbitration or taken before Mr. Rallies, the stipendiary magistrate at Liverpool —Mr. Thompson was agreeable to this coarse, but Mr. Peters ob. jected, and eventually it was agreed that the magistrates most decide the matter. Evidence was then taken emwing that defendant. besides being owner of a Ninth of the "Morn- ing Star," was also the captain. His co-owners were dissatisfied with the manner in which the defendant ful- filled his duties, alleging druokenaesa and neglect. On the 3rd S•ptember the other three owners determined to dis- pense with his services as captain, and he was given due tit 'ties by Mr Medley. On the subsequent occasions the certificate of registration was demanded, but the defendant refused to yield up the document; and during the week the defendant took the flat out of the dock, sailed it to Green- &ld and returned with a cargo of limestone. Mr. P. Speak- man, of Ruucorn, was given permission by be owners to take the stone, but after part of the cargo had been unship- ped revoked the order.—Mr. Thompson argued that the co. owners by this act had acknowledged that the voyage was a rightful one, and that a fresh notice of dismissal was necessary, and that the defendant had reasonable cause to refuse to relinquish the certificate as be had not been paid the freight of the cargo in queetion.—The Bench decided that the complainants were entitled to the certificate, and fined the defendant £l. ancreoes, 41 2s Gel, for refusing to give it up.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. Present : the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Hadfield, Hamilton, Warburton, Lewis, Aaron. Smith, Turner ; H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Farring. ton (nuisance inspector)

AN APPOINTMENT.—the Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, which sanctioned the appoint- ment until September 29th, ISBB, of Jones Farrington as inspector of nuisances, at a salary of £l4O per annum. FRODSHAM WATER SUPPLY.—A letter was read from the Public Works Loan Commissioners, agreeing to lend the Authority £475 for works of water supply, to ba repaid in rive yearly instalments of principal and interest. NUISANCES —lnspect)! Farrington reported that the action against Sir It.chard Brooke, Bart., with regard to the nuisance at Acton Grange, had been adjourned bra mouth by mutual arrangement with Mr. C. L. Evans and the Authority's soli- citor. A plan of a nine-inch sewer to Bostock-street, Stock- ton Heeth, was submitted by the Bridgewater Trueteee. No decision was arrived at on the matter. Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, wrote complaining that the state of lieckwick brook WAS injurious to the cattle drink- ing the water.—Mr. Farrington said tile brook flowed past Preston Brook Tannery. through Sir Richard Brooke's estate, and discharged into the river Mersey. When the water Wee last analysed, the analyst said that flab could live in the water, but the inspector was inclined to think that since the present tanner bad commenced operations the water was darker than it was in Mr. Prieettnan'e time. Whether it was through some new process or not he could not say.—The Clerk There is no doubt there is same fresh process. There is no pollution of that brook except from the taenery.—Mr. Farrington: No, eir.—lt was re- solved that a sample of the water ahsve and below the tan- nery should be taken and analysed. IstsPxcrort.—On tl,e proposition of the Rev. J. Lock. wood, it was resolved that Inspector Farrington should have a fortnight's holiday according to his application. The members also expressed their sympathy with Mr. Farrini,eton in the sad death of his son by accident.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Hadfield, Fisher, Turner, Hamilton, Lewis, Brandreth, Hewitt, Kirk- ham, Smith, Forster, Hall, H. Linaker (clerk.) Nia. HADFIELD l' XPLAINS —Mr. Hadfield, before the business commenced, made a personal explanation. At the last meeting something was said about the non-payment of the calls from various parts of the Union, and it was de- cided—he moved the resolution—that proceedings should be taken against the overseers and assistant overseers, giv- ing them a fortnight to ply. A letter bad been written to a contemporary crating that the gentleman who had pro- posed the resolution was himself very much behindhand in. the payment of his rates and did not pay them until they were four months past due. If that had been the case it would have been most inconsistent on his part, but the -statement in that letter was entirely wrong and incorrect. The rate was laid in June; demand notes were left in July and August. two months and one month only ago; and the assistant overseer never called for the money, and no ap- plication was made for the money. He (Mr. Hadfield) them sent a cheque for the rates, but he could not get a receipt. for the cheque for nearly ten days afterwards, and then only after a second application. He did not know whether the assistant overseer thought it W 49 not his duty after leaving the demand for the rate to call for the mosey, but as he got 10 per cent, on the amount collected, he thought he ought to do so. _

Tn CONTRACTS.—The only business of public interest was the cmsideration of the various tenders. A. committee W Tanner, Messrs. Hewitt, consisting of the Rev. J Brandreth, Fisher, Kirkham, Lewis, and Hamilton, was appointed to deal with the tenders, and on their re- commendation the following were accepted :—Grocery, J Kidd, Frodsharn ; coal, W and It Richardson, Warrington drapery, T Wright, Halton; drugs, &c., I Speakman, Run- corn: carting, W Grounds, Aston; butcher's moat, W Gill, Warrington; coffins, W Lightfoot, Aston; shoes, Jobe. Hobson, Nantwich.

FRODSTIAM. HARVEST FESTIVALS.—Parish Church; The annual its?. " vest thanksgiving service was celebrated in the above church" last evening week. Toe decorations exceeded the was!. standard of excelleoce which characterises these festivals. An appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev. J. T. Pen- rose, vicar of Crawsworth. The offertory was devoted to the funds of the Chester Infirmary, and realised over £l2. U•sion Church : The annual service in connemion with the Union Church, Frodsham ldridge, was held on Sunday even- ing, and was well attended. The chief attraction in thee decorations was the pulpit, which had been ornamented in a beautiful manner. The collections amounted to £4 lie and were in aid of the Chester and Warrington Infirmaries. Mr. Thomas Rigby preached an appropriats sermon.— Five Crosses: The annual harvest thanksgiving ssrvices were held in the Five Crosses Wesleyan Chapel on Sun- day, afternoon and evening. The chapel had been very taetef ally and beautifully decorated. The preacher was Mr. J. Beard, of Didshury College, and the collections realised 1.4 Ss 3d.

LYII3I. SIToP Ronntrny.—At the Police Court at Altrinchain, on Tuesday, Henry Birchall (17), who is employed at Massey Brook Works, was charged with having stolen a quantity of cigars and lozenges from the premises of Mr. Henshall, chemist, of Lynda,. Prisoner committed the theft when at the shop of the prosecutor. on Monday, he having h.en sent there to make a purchaso. It transpired that pris.mer had previously. been convicted, and he was now sent to Kontsford Quarter Sessions for trial. _

VOLITNT;Ett PARADE.—The H. (Lymm) Cotnpany, 3rd C It V , paraded at headquarters on Saturday, in review order, under command of Captain J. A Jones and Surg- on R. E. Williamson. Headed by the band, the company did a route march through Booth's-hill and Statham, along the S;ation-road, down Eagle-brow, and through the village to the Fleece Inn. There Captain Jones distributed the prizes to the successful competitors at the shooting about a month since. After partaking of refreshments, the corps marched back to headquarters, where, after giving up their arms for the annual inspection, they were dismissed. ROBBING A SALVATIONIST..--At the Borough Court at Warrington yesterday, a woman named Mary Elizabeth Collins, said to belong to Chester, was charged with having stolen three silk handkerchiefs, three brooches, one pocket book, some neck beads, and a purse containing a shilling, the property of Miss Stork, "captain" of the Lynun Salva- tion Army. She was remanded to the Lvmm police to be dealt with. It ssems that prisoner attende4 a farewell meeting of Salvation Army officers at Lymna, and subse- quently went to the hones of the prosecutrix. Aftec her departure the articles were missed. Prisoner was appre- hended in Warrington on Thursday evening, when the stolen articles were found in her possession.

div.head: 'THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT AT
div.p: 'THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT AT
WARRINGTON. TOWN'S MEETING.

- - - - On Tuesday evening a town's meeting of the bur- • gesses and ratepayers, convened by the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), was held in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, "to take into consideration the advisability of making the Warrington Library a free lending library, and to pass resolutions there- on." The requisition in favour of the meeting,l which was presented to the Mayor, was signed by 835 persons. The time fixed for the commencement of the meeting was seven, o'clock, but this hour, it was generally considered, was too early to allow of the punctual attendance of working-men, most of -whom are engaged at their work till six o'clock. This anticipation proved in some degree correct, for at seven o'clock the room was barely half-filled. After that time, however, the numbers rapidly in- creased, and by half-past seven there was a large attendance. After the proceedings began it was soon found that the meeting was enthusiastic and all but unanimous in favour of the project for free- ing the library. The chair was taken by the Mayor, and the others on the platform were the Rev. S. , Wilkinson, Councillor Dixon, Messrs. T. Morris, T. Birchall, J. Walker, J. Gandy, T. Flood, H. Whit- ham, and J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk.) Amongst those in the body of the hall were the Rev. J. J. Langham, Councillors A. Mackie, W. Pierpoint, J. Greening, H. Roberts, Dr. Gornall, Dr. Starkie Smith, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. A. Browne, &c. The MIYon, who was cordially received, said he had been asked to preside there that evening in ac- cordance with the requisition which had been !landed to him, signed by a very large number of names of inhabitants of the town. He did so with great pleasure, because the question of a free li- brary was one that ought to be thought of and to be well considered by every man who read a book or a newspaper. The question was one which had some difficulties. They heard that in other towns, such as' Runcorn. St. Helens, Widnes. and other places in the kingdom, they had free libraries. In Warring- ton they had what was called a free library, but books were not allowed to go out of the library to any person without payment. That payment, al- though it seemed a small amount-ss—yet it was considered by several parties in the town to be an oppressive or unjust tax on some people who could not afford it. There was no doubt there were a great many who could afford 5s a year, while others who were fond of reading books eould go to, the library and read any book they liked, but they must not take it away home with them. It was a question he had not mixed himself up in very much, but still, as there were so 'many in the town who were, he might say, rather pre- judiced in favour of that alteration, he thought it Was only proper that they should have a meeting like that to ventilate their views. (Hear, hear.) They would give the Subject their consi- deration, and in the end they would see whether or not the Corporation and the authOrities who managed the library—the Museum and Library Committee—were unjustly withholding a frbe library from the town. They knew that there was an old saying, that "money made the mare to go "—he was not alluding to himself personally. (Laugh- ter). It was an old adage, and it was a very true • one. He had also heard a tale the other day which he thought very much applied to what he himself had the pleasure of doing some few weeks ago in the Town Council, when, as chairman of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, he moved that the barricade in front of the Town Hall should be removed, and, as in the tale he was about to tell them. thty would not let him do it. They had got the barricade up, and he supposed they should next have some cannon put upon itoto keep the inhabi- tants of the town away altogether. (Laughter.) The tale went that a man was conversing with a friend , of his about their wives, and he said he could manage his wife as well as any man. "Well," said his friend, "why don't you manage her?" "Oh," he replied, " she won't let me." (Laughter.) He (the Mayor) thought that they were very much in that position. That night they had their friends on the platform all panting, and most enthusiastic to get the library free to every one in the town, but there were other people in the town who would not let them. (Laughter.) He had no doubt, how- ever, that after they had heard what the speakers had to say they ;would retire more convinced than ever that Warrington should have a free library. (Applause.) He did not know whether or not there was any gentleman present who was going to say anything in opposition, but at all events, he hoped. if there was,both parties would be heard in a proper manner, as was always the case in Warrington. (Hear, hear, and applause.) • Mr. WarrTLE then read the following letters of apology for non-attendance, viz. :-. "13, Wilson Patten-street,September 27. 1887. Dear Mr. Mayor,—l very much regret that an engagement of consi- derable importance, from which I cannot possibly break away, will prevent my attendance to-night at the tewn's meeting on the qn,stien of freeing the Public Library. May I request you to be goo,' enough to read these linos to the meeting in explanation of my absence, mad in expression of my earnest hope that the meeting will cordially carry the resolutions to be submitted in favour of the scheme. Ido not see why Warrington should fail when other towns con- spicuously succeed in placing books belonging to a library provided by the rates at the free use of the ratepayere. Everyone rejoices at the admirable condition of the institu- tion in Dold-etreet. and the only thing lacking to make it meet the public regnirements is that the Lending Library should be entirely free to all corners (ratepayers). I feel convinced that an earnest attempt to carry out this prop.ct will show its complete feasibility, and I trust that it will now very speedily and euccessfully be accomplished.—l am, yours faithfully, Jotter YONGE.—His Worship the Mayor of Warrington." 12, Winwick-road, September Mb, 1887.—Dear Mr. Morris.—Having to leave Warrington to-morrow afternoon for Londe°, it will prevent me from attending the town's meeting and seconding the resolution to-morrow night re- nectiog the Free Lending Library question. I hope yon will have a good meeting, and all present will be unanimous •in the enestion.—Yours very truly, Jogs Rustlers" Mr. T. Mounts, who was received with applause, said that he could not help remarking that they ' should come better off that night in the hands of their present chairman than they did the last time they met at a similar meeting. (Laughter.) He had pleasure in moving—" That the Town Council be requested to take immediate steps to make the Warrington Library a lending library free to all burgesses and inhabitants of the borough as is' already the case in the surrounding towns, of Wigan, St. Helens, Runcorn, Widnes, and in over a hundred other towns in the United Kingdom." (Ap- plause.) He did not suppae that any man in that I room who had ever heard or read that maxim,l "Where there's a will there's a way," but what thought that if the Museum and Library Committee had possession of any of the will the library would have been made into a free lending one some time ago. (Hear, hear.) They said that they could not make their income cover their expenditure, but he made the assertion, with all due respect to them, that if they would they could make the library free. He did not mean to say, that the library would have been so well stocked with books and the museum so well provided with rare geological and other scien- tific specimens, or that they would not have had to do without a picture or a piece of sculpture, but still he felt convinced that they should have had scores more readers and hundreds more listeners. (Hear, hear.) If they compared themselves with towns around them, and found that they had thou- sands of readers in proportion to the population. where in Warrington they had hundreds, it was only fair to infer that it was because working-men found that they could not get books so cheaply in Warring- I ton as they did elsewhere. (Hear, hear.) The more the readers the more the thinkers, and the aim of those who wanted the library free was to make it more difficult to find a fool and unintelligent man in Warrington. (Applause.) They wished also to help to tide the young over the most critical period of their lives. (Hear, hear.) They might depend upon it that the bookworm was a preferable man to the non-reader, and the thinker was far ahead of the non-thinker. Ever since they started that move- ment they had been told about the ways and means, and in a recent letter Mr. Robert Davies advises the • raising of the penny rate to three halfpence, his view being that if a rate were levied the manufacturer and the cottage owner would have to bear their part of the burden. That would be all very well in times of ordinary prosperity, but, as they knew, the manufacturers of this and other towns in Eng- land had just now bard work to make the two ends meet. They had had shrinkage of profits all over, and their business had fallen off into the bargain. The depression had not only affected manufacturers but cottage owners as well, and when a man lived upon the rents of cottages, and there was little coming in, it was hard for him to get along, and he objected to any more rates being levied upon him than could be helped (Hear, hear.) He admitted that Hr. • Robert Davies was quite right when he said to him once that if manufacturers got their men more in- telligent they would profit by it; but if they could -ot get the money out of the manufacturers they 'ld not help it, for there was no law to make' • people generous: (Laughter.) If it had not COL these

div.p: been for one magnificent old gentleman, Mr. Bea- mont, whom they all respected and admired, he very much questioned whether they would not have had a School Board in the town years ago, and that would have weighed very heavily on manufactur- ers and cottage owners. Such men as Mr. Beareont were to be admired by them all. (Hear, hear.) They were told, Mr. Morris continued, that they were trying to pauperise the workingman by free- ing the library, but he replied that the middle-clase were already being pauperised because they were allowed to have books for be a year, when they would have to pay a guinea at bindle's or Smith's library. The worlringmen paid the library rate in order that these middle-class people might save 15s a year. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Then there was another matter that should be considered. Many of the present subscribers were not ratepay- ers, because they lived outside the radial line of the borough. These people were allowed to have books for 5s a year, when otherwise they would have to i pay a guinea, while the ratepayers n the town had to pay both the 5s and the library rate. (Hear, hear.) This course did not impress- them with the idea of fair play. (Hear, hear.j. He urged„ there- fore. that from this time forth all should be treated alike, and that they should not continue to pauper- ise the middle-class by allowiitg them to have books for five shillings when, but for the rate, they would pay a guinea. He urged, also, that ratepayers should not be charged the same subscription as non-ratepayers. He asked that this sort of thing should be stopped. and that the Library Committee should do the best they could for the townspeople with the money they got from the rate, and that all should be placed on the game footing. (Applause.) He was sure that if they did this somebody would come to their assistance if they got into difficulties. (Applause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON, who was warmly re- ceived, said it seemed to him that the resolution struck the nail on the head, and he had very great pleasure in seconding it. They must all feel glad that their Mayor showed an interest in what they were trying todo, and they also thanked him for the very admirable speech with which he commenced their proceedings. • (Applause.) It was said that "comparisons are odious," but when they compared Warrington with other towns in the neighbourhood it did seem that Warrington did not compare very favourably with those towns, isecause it seemed to be lacking in one important particular. So it seemed to him as a Warringtonian—for though not born in Warrington all his interests and pleasures were connected with the town—be must confess that he was proud of the town in a great many ways. If ithey looked upon the distinguished list of Mayors, and the distinguished list ot learned men they had. had, if they looked at the work done by their Cor- poration they need not be ashamed, while he thought if they looked at the trade of the town it would bear comparison with that of other towns. Still he was sorry that, while they had a museum, library, and art gallery that were exceedingly good, they were inferior to the other towns mentioned in the resolution, inasmuch as they did not possess al free lending library. (Hear, hear.) The blayor had told them, and he believed that it was a point that interested a great number of people, that the whole ' thing to a very great extent depended on ways and 1 means. As there were other gentlemen who would go fully into that part of the subject he felt that it I was not necessary for him to say anything in the matter. A friend of his, who lives outside the town, said to him the other day that he hoped thesf would not succeed in making the library free, be- cause, he said the fact was that his sons and daugh- ters paid Sc a year to the library- and they got very great help from it. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Wilkinson) said that that was all very well, but the ratepayers I of the town should not. provide literature for people living at a distance; they slicitild not pay the cost while others got the benefit. (Hear, hear.) There WM this little fact they should bear in mind—that while they paid 5-3, for the us'e of the Warrington, Library, and while other people paid 203,a year to Mudie s or to Smith's. the latter libraries were very superior to the library they had at Warrington. They ould get a great number of books, valuable books, from the Warrington Library, but from Smith's and Mudie's libraries they could obtain all the modern books, which they could not get from the Warring- ton Library, and they could, therefore, hardly com- pare the one with the other. It seemed to him that when an effort Was made, and he trusted it would be, to make the library entirely free the cases of those ladies and gentlemen wto lived at a dis- tance, but who had paid the 53 a year should be considered, and that they might be permitted to continue their subscriptions, and, of course, gradually die off. In this manner they would aid the funds of the institution. (Hear, hear.) There was an important matter connected with the movement which Med been suggested by a friend on the platform as they were talking over the matter the other day. As the library was at present constituted, and as the reading-room now existed, there was very little help afforded to the female population. (Hear. hear.) He did not think they ever saw ladies reading in the Free Library, and it was important they should be provided with literature at home; and if the library were made ' free, and the books were allowed to be taken home, their sisters from the various parts of the town would enjoy them as much as the men could, and it would be conferring a great benefit on the house- holders of Warrington by their wives and daughters being able to have useful and improving literature for their own reading at home. He believed that free libraries did a vast amount of good. They had only to go to Liverpool and to see the lib- raries there to be thoroughly convinced cf that. The resolution was to the effect that the Tbwn Council should be requested to take immediate steps to make the Library a lending library. He sincerely hoped that the work which had been taken so earnestly in hand would not be allowed to hang fire: and that now they had begun to 'set the stone rolling they would not allow it to stop till the great work had been accomplished. (Applause.) He believed that in most things procrastination was'the thief of time, and now that they had excited the in- terest of their Mayor and other reading inhabitants of the town the scheme could be carried out if they would only take an interest in it. Their young men and young women were surrounded on every side by temptations of ell kinds, but if they could sup- ply them at home with useful literature—pleasing, reading—he believed they would stay there at night instead of rambling about the town and ' get— ting into mischief, as so many of them did. (Ap- plause.) Mr. T. FLOOD, in supporting the resolution, said that if they wanted to elevate the moral tone of the people they must make them a thinking people, make them study and read, and take an interest in the metal as well as the social life of the country, and that then there would be a hope for the rising generation. When he saw before bin? a gentleman whose voice for many years was used in defence of the working classes, he regretted very much that they bad not g-t him in the forefront now. He alluded to Dr. Mackie—(applause)—whose voice was ever raised on behalf of the working classes. When they had appealed to those whomth ey knew were abie to advocate their cause, they had been met with coldness and apathy arising from one feeling alone —a desire not to offend persons in certain quarters; but that was a feeling which should be swept aside. (Hear, hear.) It should not be a question of privi- lege or vested interest, but a question of public , right. (Applause.) They asked that that which was corporate property should be theirs, and theirs alone, and not be regulatesi and controlled by cer- tain classes. (Applause.) , He connected himself with the Free Library movement in the belief that if the work was to be carried out it must be on a certain condition, namely, that not one additional fraction should be imposed on the ratepayers, and that the burdens they already had to bear should not be increased. On that condition he allowed himself to become a member of the Cemmittee, and the figures which had been placed before him proved to his satisfaction—and they should prove to the satisfaction of an unprejudiced mind—that the library could be made free without any additional expenditure being incurred. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) To prove the honesty of the promoters of the Free Library,he might mention that bir.Thomas Morris made an offer of .£soo—(applause)--to be placed unreservedly at the disposal of the members of the Library Committee, to make an experiment Ito ascertain whether the plan of a free library was • workable ; but he was afraid that the offer came from the wrong quarter. When the Committee were further told that the £5OO would be supple- mented by at least £250. making .£750 in all, and that the whole of the money would be placed at the disposal of the Committee to work the library as a free circulating library for at least five years, it was asked "But what will you do at the end of five years?" He (the speaker) wished, however, to point out that the assessment and the value of pro- perty was increasing, and that the increased assess- ment at the end of five years would enable them to free the library; but it appeared that the library was not to be made free, owing to the fact that there were stumbling blocks in the road. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

On Thursday afternoon, a meeting of the local Ship Canal Committee was held in the Town Hall, Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. H. A. Naylor, J. Fairclough, C. J. Morris, W. Long, T. Jolley, Hutchins, J. Smethurst, C. J. Holmes, J. Geddes, J. Pierpoint, W. Owen, and J. L. Tunstall (secretary).

div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

Tig NOSE DIFFICULTY.—" The times are hard, my dear," said a man to his better half, "and I find it very difficult to keep my nose above water." "You could easily keep your nose above water," returned the lady, "if you didn't so often keep it above the brandy-and- water." BETTER THAN Passas.—Two newspaper reporters were recently killed on the Pennsylvania Central Railroad, and the personal representatives of the dead scribes have brought suits against the railroad company in each case for 10,000 dollars. In the good old days of free passes it didn't cost a railroad company anything to kill a news- paper reporter. INTERRUPTING THEIR SPORTS.—" Why—why, how is this!" said a stranger as he came up to a crowd of chil- dren engaged in a general melee; "you must stop this fighting." " Oh, let us, mister," cried a younster, checking an intended blow, and, turning on the intruder, "none o' you old folks like to see children enjoying their- selves !" AN' IT WAS HERSELF THAT HAD EXPERIENCIE.—"You say that you have only been in England three months," said a lady to an applicant for the situation of cook. "I'm afraid you haven't had experience. Were you in service before you came to this country ?" "Dade, an' I wasn't, mini; but I've had experience since I've been here. In three months I've been in half-a-dozen places. A lady once went a considerable distance to visit an intimate friend who had been taken seriously ill, but the alarming syrnptems had subsided before the anxious visitor arrived, "Oh, my dear Mrs. C., hoo are ye ?" she asked in breathless anxiety. "Oh, I'm quite wedl noo, thank ye." "Wed, said ye an me come a' this length to see ye ?" ANSWERING Pissox.—The Rev. F. A. C. Lil- lingston tells a story of a c,ateclietical address in which it was sought to lead a congregation of children to see that the wearing of a uniform was a mirk of distinc- tion, making the individue easily recognised and Invoivii4 responsibilities. "You Pee a man walking I very erect, dressed in a red coat—whd la he ?" "A 1 soldier, sir." "Right. You see a man wearing a kind of helmet, and drassed in blue—who is he ?" "A police- man, sir." "Right again." Then the preacher braced himself up to sketch a parson. "You see a man dressed in a black coat, and wearing a stiff white collar—who is he ?" "A masher, sir," was the triumphant rejoinder. ; EQUAL TO THE EMERUENCY.—A short time since a gentleman who lived in a small town not far from Buffalo went the way of all flesh, and the burial cere- monies to be performed over his remains were corn- nutted to the charge of a local undertaker. The funeral was quite an important one, for the gentleman was I prominent in his own town, and a number of his ; friends from the city were present. The services were I held in the church, but just as the time arrived for taking the. renlainl Vc the cemetery a severe thunder- steer! Came Up, and it Was considered beet not to start ' until the worst of the storm was over. The wait was ; rather an embarrassing one, but the undertaker was I equal to the emergency. Standing on the cinUCTI §tePs. I he shouted so as to be heard in the choir loft at tha other end of the building: "The organist will please I give us a little music to while away the time." Even ' the mourners smiled. This Jtioui NititnEb THE MONEY.—I have just heard the following good story an Chief Justice Bleckley. All who know Judge Bleckley and recall his long, waving hair and beard will appreciate the story. Judge Bleckley was on his way to the Supreme Court one morning, whein he was accosted by a little street gamin, with an exceedingly , dirty face, with the customary "Shine, sir ?" He was quite importunate, and the Judge, being impressed with the oppressive untidiness of the boy's face, said: "I don't want a shine, but if you go wash your face I'll give you a dime." "All right, sir." "Well, let me see you do it." The boy went over to the artesian hydrant and made his ablution. Re- turning, he held out his hand tor the dime. The Judge said: "Well, sir, you've earned your money; here it is." The boy said: "I don't want your money, old fellow; you take it and have your hair cut." Saying which he scampered off. HUMAN NATURE ON THE TRAMCAR.--" No, We don't see much of human nature on the rear platform," replied the street car conductor. "There are about so many phases, and when, you get to the end they repeat. Here is the winter list t—Am asked forty-eight times per day if it isn't pretty told work. About twenty-five passengers per day olaServe that stoves in the cars are a great im- provement. Get a blowing up from about ten females per day because the car does not stop dead in front of them. Here about twenty people per day observe that the company doesn't seem to be running cars for the benefit of the public. Am offered an average of two cigars per day by men who want about two dollars' worth of some information I haven't got. There is an average of two female dead-beats over my route each day, and there are fourteen threats per week to report me to the superintendent. One-fourth of the people who ride with me exhibit the selfishness of swine, and two-thirds ot the men ought to be kicked for the impu- dent way they stare at the women. That's about all, except that I am asked about fifty times per day if I've heard the latest."

REPORT OF DEPUTATION. The MAYOR said there had been a deputation ap- pointed from that Committee to wait on the direc- tors of the Ship Canal, and this deputation was now ready to report.—Mr. TUNSTALL then read the re- port as follows: "The deputation appointed by the Warrington General Committee of the Ship Canal on 26th May last to wait on the directors, and point out to them the reasons why the authorised scheme is not approved by the people of Warrington, now beg to present their report. In accordance with their instructions they requested (through the secretary, Mr. Tunstall,) an interview with the directors. which was granted for Friday, the 3rd June. When the deputation, at the appointed time, called at the Ship Canal office, they were in- formed that the deputy chairman and several of the directors had been suddenly called to London, but that two of their number were pre- sent, together with the secretary and the sub-engineer, and ready to receive the de- putation. A long interview followed, in course of which. those gentlemen appeared to be much im- pressed with the objections urged against the authorised scheme, and promised to lay them be- fore their colleagues. This could not be done for some time owing to the financial and Parliamentary crisis (now matter of history) through which the directors had to struggle for the very existence of the company. Wheu in course of time the crisis had been passed triumphantly, the deputation, bear- ing in mind that time and events of great import- ance must necessarily have weakened the effect of their arguments, thought it advisable to recapitu- late them in the form of a memorial to the direc- tors, embodying at the same time certain further suggestions and forming a complete alternative scheme, which, while obviating the objections, and meeting the requirements of Warrington, would probably have been completed at much less cost to the company. The deputation regret to inform the committee that the directors' answer is adverse to their memorial, and they beg to conclude their re- port by reading the memorial and the directors' reply. thereto. Signed, John Pickmere (Mayor of Warrington), John Fairclough, R. A. Naylor, Claude J. Morris, J. Hutchins, J. Pierpeillt," MEMORIAL TO SHIP CANAL DIRECFORS. Mr. TUNSTALL next read the memorial as follows :—"The anciereigned members of the deputation appointed by the Warilugton Local Committee of the Ship Canal to wait upon the directors and exellaila tet theni bow the authorised plan does not meet the approval a the manufectifeefe of the town, now beg to lay before the Board in writing the maid pointe of the cenversation so kindly heard by two of their number, together with the secretary and the sub-engineer, on ete third June last, and at the same time to offer come further euggestions springing from the said interviews. The distance a the dock proposed by the company from all the principal wades, whether east, west, or none: of the town, entails on the ownero heavy charges for carting as compared with the railways, which itt feeillif befiry ease have their etatiens (with Or Without sidings) within mode- rate distances of thole) Works. For this reason much of the traffic would gravitate to those railways, and PO be lost to the canal. The access to the dock by the old ever bridge, followed by the Level crossing over the London and North- Western Railway at Wild.erspOol Causeweyes inadequate for the present traffic, Mt therefore would be still more inade- VIM for Kee, increase and could only be supplemented by a railway or another bridge, both of which are almost im- possible, and both of which would so increase the cost of haulage of loads of Iron and other heavy goods as to render the expense of using the canal quite prohibitive. The al- ternative scheme advocated by the deputation entirely ob- viates the foregoing objections, and provides a river dock like the Clyde at Glasgow, of much greater capacity than the authorieed scheme, in the best possible position, whilst at the same time the cost would pro- bably be reduced by nearly one half. MR. MoRLEY AT NEWCASTLE.

Mr. John Morley addressed his constituents on ; Saturday night in the Town Hall, Newcastle-on- Tyne. The hall was crowded, and Mr. Morley met , with an enthusiastic reception. The right hon. , gentleman at the outset disposed of the rumour that he was about to retire from public life because Mr. Gladstone was not enough in earnest for him. He assured his constituents that he was not at all likely to desert Mr. Gladstone unless Mr. Gladstone deserted the cause of freedom, justice, and good government in Ireland. He still adhered to his propositions fist, that they ShOUld create a Legta/aturei rel4n4i :espfisitle to Irish public opinion, dealing with affairs which Parliament `,..termines to be exclusively Irish, and secondly, that the land question must be effectively settled before or along with the settlement of the political I question. A new controversy had, he said, arisen, which was whether Ireland was to be governed as a free country with a free constitution, or whether it was to be ruled by an arbitrary and violent Govern- ment. Mr. Morley dealt with the Crimes Bill, and contended that a more wanton, more gratuitous. more unprovoked, and more mischievous provoca- tion was never offered to a nation. It now seemed 'as if they were going to see wry bad law vory ! badly administered. He complained that the Go- vernment in the line they had taken were putting the cause of order and authority in the wrong, and no Government could be guilty of a worse crime. As to the doubtful piece of work at Mitchelstown, he asked, was there ever an occasion when a res- ponsible Minister should have been very wary or I very vigilant or more in earnest in probing the mat- I ter to the bottom? Yet the Chief Secretary did not I hesitate to form a complete and settled judgment lon an unverified and one-sided statement of facts. The course taken by the Government might drive discontent beneath the surface and show a state of sham, superficial order, but it would not lead to union between the two peoples or to a reconcilia- tion. He counselled patience on the part of the I Irish. The provocation was great, but so would the reward of patience be great. There was only one thing that could put back the cause, and that was crime and outrage. A resolution was passed con- demning the em-ployment of indiscriminating force to suppress -political meetings in Ireland as sub- versive of the most cherished conditions of consti- tutional government and destructive of every hope of true union between the peoples of the United I Kingdom.

LORD R. CHUEICIDiL.—The "Dublin Express London correspondent has reliable authority for stating that Lord ituridolph Churchill will shortly rejoin the Government. Whether he will immediately become leader of the House of Commons is uncertain, but that event would follow shortly after the opening of the session.

Dump Fut. SUICIDE AT BOLTON.-012 Friday morning a dreadful suicide was discovered to have taken place in the Hare and Hounds Public-house. Bolton. A middle-aged man, supposed to be a commercial traveller, had been stay. ina at that house since Monday, but was evidently in 15 or- tan e 4 circumstances, having bor-owed money for food. On Friday morning he was found in bed with his throat cute and x razor iyin a near. He is as yet unidentified. DISTURBANCE AT ALDERSHOT.—The Aldershot correspon- dent of the C-ntral News telegraphs that serious discontent, verging on mutiny, be broken out among a portion of V Battery, First Brigade, Royal Artillery. Twelve men have been made prisoners for disobedience, and pickets are in search of ethers who have absented themselves without leave. Some of the batery harness has been Cut by the men, who urge harsh treatment in extenuation ref their conduct.

BELGRADE, FEIDAY.—The tinal result of the elections to the Skupichina WAS not issued until seven o'clock this morning. Seventy-one Liberals and seventy Radicals have been elected, not a single member of the Opposition obtain— ing a seat.

div.p: THE YACHT RACE-SECOND STAGE.

NEW YORK, FRIDAY, 2 30.—The Volunteer (American), is now homeward boned. Th. sea is turbulent and the wind bluvring a gale. The Taistle (Scotch) is labonring heavily and bruises her bpwa dreadfully, her decks being washed from stem to stern. She is evidently carrying too much sail. The Volunteer rides the swell gracefully, and is two miles ahead.

div.head: LATER.
div.p: LATER.

_ The Volunteer arrived at Scotland Lightship, the win- ning point, at 4-22, winning easily. The Duke of Cambridge, who arrived at Manchester on Friday afternoon, opened the new head quarters of the 20th Lancashire Volunteers.

div.head: LIBRARY QUESTION.
div.p: THE LIBRARY QUESTION.

Yesterday. afternoon *are was a special meeting, of the Warrington Library and Museum Committee to take into consideration the resolutions passed at the Public Meeting on Tuesday evening last. The committee proceeded to direct their attention to the legal side of the case, and the various Acts of Par- liament were looked through and considered, begin- ning with the Museums Act of 1845. There is a fair sprinkling of lawyers on the committee, and the Town Clerk was present to give the committee the benefic of his advice. There was, as might be expected, a considerable difference of opinion as to whether the committee were legally warranted in giving privileges to subscribers; and it was ulti- Imately decided, we understand, to take counsel's opinion.

We may state that the last Act—an" Act to amend the Public Libraries Acts "—was passed as late as August Bth in this year; but we are not in a position to say whether or no it came within the purview of the committee. We were under the impression that the bill had been dropped, but it is satisfactory to find that it has become law. Its main object is to extend the Libraries Acts so as to enable small villages and parishes to erect, establish, and maintain a lend- ing library without providing any separate building for containing the same." By this Act the rate of id in the pound, though it bring in a small sum; will enable a village to maintain a "lending li!trary." We must bestir ourselves, or we may find, as to the loan of books, that we are left in the rear by Pen- keth, Padgate, Winwick, Grappenhall, &c. The "Blackburn Times" comments on the local situation as follows : A curious question has arisen in connection with the Warrington Free Library which we, who are not immediately concerned with it, can study with much interest. If any attempt were made to rob the public of Blackburn of their Free Library, and limit its use 'to a small circle of ladies and gentlemen who could afford to subscribe to it, we might be too indignant to take much pleasure in studying the situation, and we are bound to sympathise with the people of Warring- ton, who are called upon to pay a penny rate for the support of a Library which is not free to all the ratepayers, but subverted to. the select few who have combined to make it into a Subscription Library, and reserve its chief benefits to themselves. It seems strange that such things should happen in a Lan- cashire town, but we learn from the local newspapers that this is so, and we are informed that under an Act passed during the session of Parliament just ended, or some other Act, not mentioned, the War- rington Free Library Committee claim the right of giving preference to subscribers and yet calling upon the ratepayers in genersl to support it with a penny rate. Blackburn and Darwen people would not tolerate this fast and loose play with their Free Libraries, on which such great store is set, and we fancy that the men of Warrington,. being " Lancashire lads" like ourselves, will know the why and the wherefore before they permit a select few to monopolise their common rights.

He could remember when it was pure and full of fish, but now nothing would live in it betwixt there and War- ringtou.—Mr. Terry afterwards proceeded, in company with the other gentlemen present, to inspect the tile of the scheme, with a view to reporting to the Local Government Board in due course.

PRESCOT B)ARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on hursday afternoon, when there were present—Mr J Fisber (Chairman), MessrsC B Johnson, J Leatberharrow, J Ken. wrigbt, J Ranson, T Eatock, W Middleburst, J Brickley, W Swift, W Tyrer, J Barchall, E Syder, W 0 Ashton, W it Longton, itA. Graves. J Lowe, P Longton ; and S H Hart- ley (clerk). . .

'RBLIEF:—Mr. Hale, the Workhouse master, reported there were 480 inmates of the house this week, 40 last week, and 495 in the corresponding week la* year 76, vagrants had been relieved, against 79 in the corresponding week last year.
WATER Taw.—The Workhouse Master reported that twojwater tanks. constructed by Messrs R. 11. Dillies and Co., were not water-tiebt, and he had written to Mr. Davies accordingly._ _

THE 1.)-oet- Errs.—Mr. Ranson asked if the man Hancock, who hAd been bitten by a mad dog,. had yet been discharged from the Workhouse.—The Clerk said he did not think so. —Mr. Ranson : Toe dog is all right. I dent know how the man is.

Tam Ulnas °monies GIIMIANTEII9.-A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated the 17th Septem- ber, in reply to one by the clerk inquiring whether the Guardians would be authorised to pay oat Atha poor's rates the premiums upon policies of a guarantee so- ciety, to be accepted on behalf of Union offi- cers. The Local Government Board referred them to a letter addressed to Mr. Martin in regard to a similar ap- plication on the 15th June, 1874, and to state that as pointed out in that letter the Guardians-could not, in the opinion of the Board, legally pay the premiums- on guaran- tee policies-of their officers. They pointed, oat, however, that if, under the circumstances, the Guardians deemed it desirable to recommend increases in the salaries- of the officers to cover expenses- entailed upon them by the ar- rangements suggested the Local Government Board would be prepared to give the proposal their favourable considera- tion. The LocAl Government Board wished to know if the Guardians had called upon their inquiry officers to give security.—Tho Clerk suggested that the letter should be referred to the Finance Committee, and the suggestion was adopted.

A SWEEPING, MACHINE.—The Clerk reported the receipt of the following communication September 29tb, 1887: —Gentlemen of the Board,—lt is upwards of 12= months since I applied to the Board for the grant of a sweeping machine, as that trade was formerly my oastomary calling for a number of years. / think I could make a tolerable living for myself and family It I war furnished witli,a machine. If my application should meet the approval of the Board I should be most humbly and thankfully obliged. —Tam, gentlemen, yours, kn., PETER SIXSIEITELP-The Clerk remarked that the Guardians could not do that. They had a similar application before them 12: months ago, and they refused it.. THE Coox. AND Beier —A letter was received from. Mr. Richard Grattan, cook and bakerat the Workhouse • stating that after a service of nearly four years he.venturedio ask for an increase in his wages. He desired to point out that his duties required.a constant attendance from before six o'clook•in the morning until after the same hour in the evening, Sundays included. He hoped they would consider his conduct and attention to business warranted his troubling them with the application. Ha was doing his beet to give them every satisfaction' and had.no doubt they would think him worthy of a little further encouragement. —The letter was referged to the Finance Committee. THE COUNTY' PRECEPT—The Clerk.reported that' he had net yet been able to haver' interview with the county authorities with reference tothe county precept and the charges for the police at St. Helens: He had to ask the Gnardians to authorise the drawing of a cheque toy £6,043 12s, demanded by thenounty. There were two items which "would have to be temporarily advanced by the overseers until they could vet special rater levied in the townships of Eccieston and Windle. So. far as he could make out it would be necessary for the overseers to levy special rates in Ecclestea and Windle.—The Chairman:. Why those two townships P—The Clerk: Ihicause they are part in the borough of St. Helens, and tt would be unfair to nquire the whole of the people to pay two constabulary charges—The Guardians acceded to the clerk's-request:

A MYSTRIZIOUS DISAPPZARexcie.—The Clerk read the following letter Park-road. Bt. Ann's. Dear e.r,—ln , reply to your favour of tbe 16th instant I beg to state that I Cannot account for the nott-receipt of the monthly state- ment for August for township of Ecoleston. They were fnade out and sent by post along with those for. the town- ship of Knowsley. By this post 1 forward copy. Yours . truly, T. Parkinson."—The Clerk: The others have not reached me vet.

MEDICAL FEES.—The Cleritceported that Dr. Coeper had written to the Guardians with reference tocevaralcases of extra medical fees, and the matter had been referred to the committee, bet they had not met sicce the receipt of the letter.

THE WORKHOUSE CHAUEL.—T he Clerk said•that some time ago the Visiting Committee recornmended,tbat esti-- mates be obtained for the painting of the inside of the chapel. Three tenders bad been received.—The Board referred them to the Waiting Committee. THE Poou LAW CONFERENCE.—M r. C. B. &Almon, ~ in accordance with notice of motion, moved the appointment of a deputation from the Board to attend the Northern Poor Law Union Conference, at Manchester, on the 7th and Bth October. He slid he thought the Conferences were of grett usefulness, and there had been a satisfactory outcome of those held in the past. —Mr. W. Middlehurst seconded the motion, which was unanimously passed.—On the mo- tion of Mr. Betook, seconded by Mr. Buckley, Messrs Fisher (chairman), Johnson, Leatherbarrow, and the Clerk, were appointed the deputation. THE BOARD,MEETINGS:—The Chairman announced that, in.future, in accordance with the resolution, passed some time ago, the Board would meet at half .past ten o'clock in the forenoon. This was the only business.

div.head: NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLING, CLUB:
div.p: NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLING, CLUB:

An interesting gathering to celebrate the closing oft the season in connection with the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club was held at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Saturday tight. A. large company sat down to a substantial repasa, after which Mr. T. Stone, of Newton Park, president of-the olub, occupied the chair, and he was supported by Wears. W. Urquhart, W. D. Burdis, Liptrot, E. Edwardson, and other gentlemen. During the evening the Chairman distri• buted prizes to 4.5 members of the Bowling Club who had won them during the year. The usual loyal toasts were duly honoured.—The Chairman gave the toast of "Health of the patrons," coupling therewith the names of Lord Gerard, Mr. W. a Legh, and Mr. T. W. Legh, M.Th.. He observed that the lute Lird Gerard bad always been a good supporter of the club, and there was no doubt the present Lord Gerard would- become equally so. Mr. Legh had been very good in granting the use of the ground for the small sum of 2s 6d per year; and in regard to his generosity Mr. T. W. Legh was following in his father'a footsteps. (An- ' please.)—The toast was drunk with musical bonours,Mr. R. Lythgoe giving a capital song.—Mr. E. Faircleugh next proposed the toast et "The health of the captains of the cricket and bowling," and said tbe captains had fulfilled 1 their duties in a very creditable manner daring the year.— The toast was enthusiastically drunk.—The Chairman ob- served that he was one of the captains of the club, but had not much to do with the duties, and he would call upon another to respond.—Mr. H. J. Longton, captain of the cricket team, thanked them for the compliment they had , paid to the captains, and said that during the past i season they bad played eight matches,. winning one, losing three, and drawing four. They most confess that they had a weak first eleven, but for next year they were trying to secure a better eleven, and heped their efforts would be sue-. easeful. (Applause.)—Mr. A,. W. Tattersall, captain of the 1 second eleven, also responded, and said that team had had a. I most successful season, out of eleven matches having won eight and two being drawn in their favour. (Applause.)— Mr. Liptrot responded on behalf of the Bowling Club, and said the bowlers could hold their own against any other bowlers in the country. They had Oared three matches, and won handsomely. (Applause.)—Mr. W. Urquhart,, Mr. Bodrner, and Mr. Williams also responded.—Mr. T. Stone then sang " Pine old English gentleman" in good style, and was warmly applauded.—The Chairman gave the toast, " Health of the secretaries." He remarked that a great deal I depended upon the secretaries. and their present officials 1 had worked hard to promote the success of the club. (An- plause.)—Mr. W. H. Hindley, in responding, said they had always had great pleasire in doing all they possibly could tto promote the interests of the club.—Mr. Grace (corres- I ponding secretary) also responded, and thanked them for the kind manner in which they had drunk their healths.— Mr. E. Edwardson and Mr. T. Howard next gays songs, and Mr. W. D. Burclis. in proposing "The health of the , presi- dent " said Mr. Stone had fulfilled those duties in a noble , , manner. He had supported the club in a generous man- ner, and he was heart and soul in its success. No one in the district was a greater lover of outdoor sports or had done more to bring honour to the districts. He wished long 1 life and prosperity to Mr. Stone, and hoped he would be I President for many years in the future. (Applause.)—The 1 toast was drunk amid much enthusiasm, and Mr. Bodmer sang,—The President, on rising to respond, was warmly received. He said he was very much obliged to them for their kind expressions, and the way in which they had re- ceived the toast. Be felt he had not been able to do jug- ; tice to the position he occupied, as he had °illy been on the I ground three or four times during the year, but if it was I their wish that he should remain president he would do so, I 1 and he would endeavour to do more in the future than he I i had done in the past. (Applattse.)—The proceedings shortly afterwards terminated.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT. j
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT. j
23, Old Broad-etreet, B.C.

The Stock Exchange has again experienced a strong at- tack of depression, the " Bears " having had it all their own way. At one time it looked as though a better state of things was about to establish itself, but for purposes of the settlement prices were knocked down all round, and have not yet fully recovered. Three members of the Stook Ex- change were declared defaulters at the close of the settle- ment. With the turn of the quarter and the prospect of ease in the mosey market, the immediate future ought to show a marked improvement. If the railway roturns only Continue favourable a rise all round should be looked for. Southern irailwaya. such at Brighton A's and Dover A's, are almost entirely dependent upon the traffic returns. As far as Brighton A's are con- cerned, there is every reason to expect an increase, with a concurrent rise in prices. Investors in railways should therefore buy Brighton A's, as they are almost certain to reach 122 before the close of the current year, and at the present time they are 117, and a general rise may be looked for. One of the most melancholy declines of any railway company is the Metropolitan and District, shareholders of which must be at their wits end to see any probable im- provement. Another declining investment which shows no sign of re- covery is Copper Mining Co's. By quarters and halves Rio Tintos and Mason and Barry go down until they have reached a point not even dreamed of even a year ago,and the end has not yet been reached. To-day Rio Tintos are eight last year they stood at thirteen. On the other hand the leading borne industries in the important trading districts In the North of England show marked signs of improve- ment, and the autumn is likely to be a busy time in coal, iron and steel industries. The first sign of any movement in the companies' world was made on Wednesday in the Issue of the prospectus of a company to take over a paper mill. The advent of this company is the herald of many that may be expected dur- ing the autumn months. At a meeting of the shareholders of the Moldocott Sewing Machine Company, held on Monday, the directors were obliged to admit that the machine was an impetfect see, and for all real practical purposes is of little valne. The next scene in this company's affairs is likely to be the law courts.

SAD FATALITY AT A. WIGAN COLLIERY.-011 Monday, a fatality happened at the Taylor Pit, Standish. of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company. A man named Joseph Banks and three others were making ready for bricking the arch of the tunnel, when the roof gave way. Banks was buried beneath the debris. His fellow•workrnen got bun out, but life was extinct.

WIIMAL Foal, SHow.—Amongst the judges at a foal show held on Monday in connection with the Wirral Farmers' Club were Mr. W. II hitlow, of Preston Brook, and Mr. J. F... Wood, of Newton-le- Willows.

BOWLING AT BANE QUAY.-A main of bowls was played on the Bank Quay Bowling Green (proprie- tor. Mr. R. Mellor), on Saturday, by 32 players, the entrance fee being Is each. The weather was favourable, and there was a fair number of specta- tors present. The main resulted as follows :-Ist prize, W. Gleave, pair of bowls and 8s; 2nd, Edward Gleave, lOs ; 3rd, Joseph Webb, 4s; 4th, James Shaw, 4s; four prizes of is 64 each, 6s. CADISHEAD AND limem.— The anniversary and Harvest Taanksgiving Services were held in the Congregational Chapel, on Sunday. A Service of , Song was given in the afternoon at 2-30 entitled "Harvest Home." The reader was the Rev. Alfred Buckley, of Knutsford, and he also preached in the evening at 6-30. The chapel was decorated with great taste, and looked very pretty and becoming. The congregations were large, and collections were made at the close of each Service in aid of the Chapel Funds, amounting to £ll. THE SALE OF MILIC—At the Borough Court, on Monday, Ralph Winstanley, of 41, Old-road, Latch- ford, appeared before the magistrates to answer a summons charging him with having sold milk under circumstances not allowed by the Dairies, &c., Act of 1885. It was- stated that defendant, a retailer of milk, kept it in a shop used as a general provision storerwhich, that Rot being a proper place for the storage of milk,. wan an offence against the in cluding costs. The Bench inflicted a fine of 2s &1,, costs.

- A 13by's,A1-VEN-rurto.—OtiTuesday evening a lad, obviously a sttanger, was seen wandering about the streets and, the attention of the police having been directed, to him, he was questioned. It thereupon transpired that the lad was named Walter Lawton, whose parents live at Eccles., and that he had run away from home, taking.with him a sum of .£3 15s, which, he-took from a drawer in his parents' house. The parents were communicated wiby telegraph, and on Wednesday morning, the 'WC who is only teü years old, was given over to the care of his father. •
