Davies. THE WAY, TO SPREAD DisnAsE.—At the Borough Court. on,Monday, a married woman named Jose- ' phine Griffiths, who lives ituSharp-street, was sum- moned for taking lodgers without having her house registered, It was stated in evidence that nine persons-lived in the house, five of whom were lod- 'gen, and there were also in the place twelve geese, twelve ducks, twenty-three hens,, and thirty chickens. The premises were in. a most filthy con- dition.—The Mayor:' A regular N-oah's Ark t—De- fendant. who. said she -was badly off, and that her husband was in a lunatic asylum, was fined 58 and costs. CHESHIRE LINSWAERINGFION WORKS CRICKET ClA:.—The first annual supper in connection with the above club was held on Thursday evening at the Griffin Hotel, Horsemarket-Street, where an ex- cellent spread was provided. After the removal of the cloth Mr. Evans Was called to the chair, and Mr. Tarbock to the vice-chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were given and heartily received. Sono were ably rendered by Messrs. Tarbuck' Whitham, Foss, Langhorn, Norbury, Mercer, and Cosgrove. Mr. Warhurst„the• honorary secretary, in response to the toast of success to the C.L.O Cricket Club, rendered a.very *satisfactory statement as to its financial position. A. very 14easant even- ing was brought to a. close by singing the National Anthem. RUNAWAY ITALisam—lnformation VW received by the borough police, on Wednesday, to the effect that three Italians had absconded from Manchester, and the sum of 10s-was offered by the parents as a reward for the discovery, of their whereabouts. Their names and descriptions. were :—" Antonia Petrello, aged 18: had with hiin a monkey dressed in red; Giovanni Demarco? aged,l4', has an accordeon with him ; ,Rafello Petrellb,,,aged 15, plays an accordeon." On the evening Of the same day Constable Monoghan heard the soundt of an accordeon in the neighbour- hood of Mark ea Gate,. He went there and found two. lads, one with a monkey andthe other with an accordeon. They rue I.bled the description received from Manchester, and the constable entered into conversation with them. The result was that they admitted that they. were Antnnio Petrello and, Gidvanni Demarco,. two of the missing lads. They were detained, but not locked up; until Thursday, when they were taken back to Manchester by a relative.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday. Sep. 24th, 1887.—The , mean temperature was 52 Fehr., and therefore ldeg. warmer than the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature,. 84. Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 18th inst., and the minimum temperature, 40 Fahrenheit, on the 18th inst. The rainfall I measured nil. The general direction of the wind was S.B. • During the week, which was the 38th of the current year, 27 births and 8 deaths I were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to B'T per 1,000, against 18.0 the average of the previous 4 weeks, and against 26-9 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included, I from diarrlicea, 2. from lung disease, 1 from syphilis, 1 from brain. disease, 1 from old age, 1 from liver disease. Two, eases of scarlet fever, 2of typhoid fever, and three of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN H. GORNALL. Medical Officer of Health. CLAIM BY AN BAILLUTOWN TRAbB2MAN. At Warrington County Court, on Thursday afternoon, John Riley, greengrocer, and furniture remover, Earlestown, sued George Clough, railway servant, for the sum.of £6,.alleged to be due for goods sup- plied, motiey lent, and the removalof furniture. Mr. P. Davies- appeared for the plaintiff, who detailed the various items which made up the stun total, and who said that since a summons was taken out the defendant's wife and children had gone to Ripon, where all their goods had been removed to, and that the defendant himself was now living in lodgings in Earlestown.—Defendant, who is brother to Mrs Riley, wife of the plaintiff, said that the matter arose out of a family quarrel.—His Honour remarked that defendant seemed to have received great kind- ness from his sister and her husband, and should at least have endeavoured to pay something.—Defen, dank : They 11,5.ve received great kindness from me. as well ; I dispute the debt.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff, less 17s 6d, money which was not proved to have been lent to the de- fendant.

CONCERT A. 7 LATcnroun.—At the Temperance !fall at Latchford on Monday evening, the members of the Manchester and District Concert Assc• 2iation gave a concert before a large and appre- ciative audience. The proceeds are to be devoted to the Latchferd Temperance Society, and the services of the contributors to the programme were gratuit- ous. It had been announced that Dr. Gornall would. preside, but as that gentleman was not able to be present, Mr. Hartley was asked, and consented, to take the chair. In the course of a few introductory remarks, he said that the object which :the gentle- men connected with that building had in view was a very praiseworthy one, ton everyone, must admit that the cause of temperance, which was steadily growing, was a noble one. The programme was then proceeded witl ~ and it soon became evident that the concert was of a high-class character. The artistes were Miss. Agnes Whitehouse (soprano), Miss Whitehouse (mezzo-soprano.); Mr. Tucker (tenor), Mr. F. Hopkinson, Southport (bass), Mr. William Adams, of Ardwick, concertina soloist, and gold and silver medallist. Mr. R. Hopkinson, organ- ist of St. Mark's, Gorton, was the pianist. During the evening there were several recalls, and the efforts of the artistes were much appreciate& At , the conclusion of the proceedings the Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies and gentle- men who had given their services. In seconding the motion, Mr. Ellison also proposed a vote of I thanks to the chairman for presiding. He, as a member of the Temperance Society, thanked all who had assembled to help them in their temper- ance work. He believed that they had made the neighbourhood better, that there were less drunk, ards, and they were trying to train up the children in temperance principles. They had ap present over one hundred members in the Juvenile Temperance Order, and he hoped that these would in the future take the places of the elder one. Both resolutions were then passed and acknowledged, and the .pro- ceedings concluded with the singing sat the. Natlonal Anthem.

The Company has been formed for the purpose of insuring agaivat loss of principal or interest the holders of mortgages upon real and personal proper y, and it is contemplated that its principal operations shall relate to securities upon property in and near Liverpool. The Company is also empowered to grant insurances for securing mortgage debentures, debenture stock, and other securities or a similar character. The wide scope which exists for the Company's operations Is shown by the following facts :—it has been ascertained from reliable sources that the gross rental of the rate,ble property in Liverpmi and the surrounding districts on both sides of the Mersey exceeds £6,000,000 per ant um. The capital value of this property, calculated at an average 01 15 years' purchase upon the gross rental, is estimated to hoover £90,000,1)00. It Is believed, as the result of numerous inquiries, that at least two-thirds of this property, representing a value of £60,000,000 or thereabouts, is subject to mortgages. If, as is usually the case, the average armtust lent upon the mortgaged pr-sporty be two-thirds of the estimated value, the aggregate of existing mortgages upon property in Liverpool and the immediate ' neighbourhood would approximately represent a sum of over ' £40,000,000. Few securities have occupied a higher place as regards safety in the estimation both of private investors and of trus- tees than mortgages of land and buildings, and this position has, as a rule, been justified whenever a rine margin of value over and above the amount lent ha, been required, and ordinary precautions have been taken to distinguish properties which have been well lonia and not over vamed from those which do not answer to this description, or which are from Various Causes of an exceptionally risky character. The experience of solicitors and agents who have most to do with securities of tins class shows taut comparatively few losses are incurred when reasonable care has been exercised In their original relecti in, especially where t'ae investor cr his agent has brought to bear upon such selection a fair local knowledge of the dist let in which the property is situated. The instances of loss have been extremely few where the mortgaged property, bssides having been carefully selected in the first instance, has been periodically inspected, so that any depreelatiori or want of repair has been detected at an early stage. The ordinary course of the Company's business would be to receive from the lender on mortgage, or in some cases from a proposed borrower, a proposal for insuring the lender against loss of principal, interests, sod costs The proposal would be accompanied by a statement of particulars of the proposed security, and a valuation by some approved professional valuer. The proposal would theo be considered by the Com- pany after an Investigation by their officers, and, if accepted, an annual premium of insurance would be charged, varying according to the nature of the risk taken from a minimum rate of one-eighth per cent upon the principal sum assueed. A policy would then be issued guaranteeing the holder: under specified conditions, and providing for a transfer? to the Com- pany of al the rights possessed by the mortgagee upon their satisfying his claim under the pol.cy. The promoters are of opinion that if they succeed in Obtaining insurances in respect of even one-tenth part of the property mortgaged -in Liverpool and the neighbourhood, a good return by way of dividend may be expected by the share- holders. They look forward, howeve,. to doing a much larger business, and it is hoped that in course of time, when the public become sufficienty acquainted with the advan- tages of the system of insurance now proposed, the Company's policies will become an ordinary requirement to mortgagees when accepting a mortgage. It may be added that in the rare cases in which losses maybe actually sustained by the Com- pany the amount of such losses will, from the nature ot the security, naturally bear only a small proportion to the sum assured. No contracts affecting the Company have been entered into, and no promotion money has been or will be paid. The pre- liminary expenses will be limited to the necessary legal charges, stamp duties, and other ordinary disburse,nents. If no allotment is made the application money will be returned in full. and in case a smaller amount is allotted than is applied for, the excess paid on application will be applied in Payment of the allotment money. Prospectuses and forms of application for snares may be obtained from the eeeretary, at the offices of the Company, and from the Bankers, Brokers, and Solicitors of the Com- pany.
